drills.name: Easy cardio warm-up
equipment: exercise bike, rower, cross-trainer or treadmill
drills.summary: Continuous easy-to-moderate cardio that opens every session. It raises muscle temperature, heart rate and breathing before anything else, which matters more for you than for most people because you train about an hour after waking.
drills.dose: Default 6 min: start at [[term:rpe|rating of perceived exertion (RPE)]] 2-3, finish at RPE 4-5 (breathing faster, still able to talk in sentences). Upper day: rower or cross-trainer. Lower days: bike or incline walk. Cardio day: 4 min easy on the machine you will use. Interval day: 8 min (4 easy, 4 at RPE 5). Run day: 5 min brisk walk. Test day: 8 min, progressive. Take 8 min on cold days or when you feel stiff. Log it in Hevy as cardio (machine, minutes).
setup: Rower or cross-trainer before upper-body work; bike or incline walk before leg work.
A timer on the machine or phone is enough; no heart-rate monitor needed.
execution: First half very easy (RPE 2-3).
Second half: add resistance, speed or incline until breathing is clearly faster but full sentences are still possible (RPE 4-5).
Go straight on to the mobility drills without sitting down.

errors.error: Turning it into a workout (RPE 7 or more).
errors.fix: Cap it at RPE 5; the job is temperature, not fitness.

errors.error: Skipping it because the gym is hot.
errors.fix: A warm room is not working muscle: passive heating was largely ineffective as a warm-up for upper-body performance [@McCrary2015_upperbody_warmup].

drills.progression: No load progression. As fitness improves the same RPE needs more speed or resistance; follow RPE, not the display.
drills.regression: Stay at RPE 2-4 throughout if 6 min leaves you breathless.

alternatives.why: From [[phase:p2]], easy skipping can replace the last 1-2 min for variety.

drills.whyChosen: In one study, performance (including grip strength) followed biological time and habitual sleep timing rather than clock time [@FacerChilds2018_chronotype], so a session an hour after waking probably behaves like an early-morning one, when average force was 2.6-3.3% and peak velocity 11.5-13.6% lower than in the evening [@Pullinger2019_morning_warmup_lifts] (applying this to you is inference). See [[dec:D10]].
drills.safety: For chest pain, dizziness, palpitations or unusual breathlessness, stop and follow [[plan:safety]]. In hot weather stay at RPE 4-5 and drink water (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: Cross-bridge cycling, myosin ATPase activity, sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium handling and nerve conduction all speed up as muscle warms, and warm connective tissue resists lengthening less (background physiology, not measured in the cited trials). Temperature is only part of it: a long morning warm-up that brought rectal temperature to evening levels did not restore evening lifting performance [@Pullinger2019_morning_warmup_lifts], so neural activation and rehearsal probably matter too (inference).
drills.evidence: Warm-ups improved performance in 79% of outcomes across 32 studies, with little sign of harm [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance]. Adding 20 min of easy cycling to a specific warm-up raised leg-press [[term:1rm|one-repetition maximum (1RM)]] by 8.4% in trained people [@Abad2011_general_specific_warmup]. Warm-ups reduced time-of-day performance differences, extended morning warm-ups most [@Kusumoto2021_diurnal_variation]. A 10-min uphill-walk warm-up cut soreness 48 h after unaccustomed exercise by 13 mm on a 100-mm scale [@Law2007_warmup_cooldown_DOMS]. The 6-min default is a compromise, not a tested optimum.

drills.name: Leg swings (front-back)
equipment: wall, rack upright or machine frame to hold
drills.summary: Relaxed pendulum swings of one leg forward and back, growing gradually larger. A [[term:dynamic-stretching|dynamic stretching]] drill that loosens your tight hamstrings and hip flexors before lower-body work without the strength cost of long static holds.
drills.dose: 10 swings per leg, left leg first, in full-body A, lower-day, athletic lower-day, cardio, interval, run and test warm-ups. Swings 1-3 small, then gradually larger.
setup: Stand side-on to a support and hold it with the near hand; stand on the right leg so the left leg swings first.
Stand tall; standing knee slightly bent, swinging knee soft.
execution: Swing the free leg forward and back, letting momentum do the work.
Widen the arc over the first few swings; stop the forward swing at a mild hamstring stretch, not a pull.
Keep pelvis and trunk still; the motion is at the hip.
Turn round and repeat on the right leg.

errors.error: Kicking to end range with a locked knee.
errors.fix: Keep the knee soft and let range build over the 10 swings; your hamstrings set the limit.

errors.error: Rounding the back to get the leg higher.
errors.fix: Lower the arc until the trunk stays upright.

drills.progression: Range grows by itself. Once easy, let go of the support for the last 3 swings to add balance demand.
drills.regression: Smaller arc, or bend the swinging knee more.

alternatives.why: Hip flexors and hamstrings in a lunge if no support is free.
Where hamstring flexibility is actually built: static holds after the session ([[dec:D27]]).

drills.whyChosen: You cannot touch your toes, and Romanian deadlifts and lunges need hip-flexion range from the first set. Swings prepare that range now; static hamstring stretching is kept for after the session.
drills.safety: Hold the support throughout, especially when standing on your weaker left leg. Stop with sharp pain at the back of the thigh or in the groin.
drills.mechanism: Swings raise local temperature and let the nervous system accept more range: short-term range gains are mostly increased [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]] rather than a longer muscle [@Weppler2010_sensory_theory]. They are not a long-term flexibility tool: chronic static and PNF stretching gained more range than ballistic or dynamic stretching [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM].
drills.evidence: Immediately after dynamic stretching performance rose about 1.3%, versus -3.7% after static stretching (-4.6% with 60 s or more per muscle) [@Behm2016_acute_stretching]. For acute [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]], stretching was no better than other warm-up activity (ES 0.01) [@Warneke2024_FR_stretch_warmup_ROM], and stretching programmes did not prevent injury (RR 0.96) [@Lauersen2014_injury_prevention]. The 10-swing dose is practical convention.

drills.name: Leg swings (side-to-side)
equipment: wall, rack upright or machine frame to hold
drills.summary: Relaxed swings of one leg across the front of the body and out to the side, growing gradually larger. A [[term:dynamic-stretching|dynamic stretching]] drill for the inner and outer hip that covers the sideways plane that [[ex:wu-leg-swing-fb]] misses.
drills.dose: 10 swings per leg, left leg first, in the full-body B, lower-day and test-day warm-ups. Where both swing drills appear, do these straight after the front-back swings.
setup: Face the support and hold it with both hands, feet hip-width apart.
Stand on the right leg so the left leg swings first; standing knee slightly bent.
execution: Swing the free leg across in front of the standing leg, then out to the side.
Start small and widen the arc over the first 3-4 swings; stop the outward swing at a mild stretch in the inner thigh.
Keep the hips square to the support and the trunk upright; the motion comes from the hip.
Swap legs and repeat.

errors.error: Tilting the trunk sideways so the swing looks bigger.
errors.fix: Shorten the arc until the shoulders stay level.

errors.error: Rotating the pelvis to follow the leg.
errors.fix: Keep the belt buckle pointing at the support; a smaller swing is fine.

drills.progression: Range grows by itself within the set. Once easy, hold on with fingertips only so the standing leg balances more.
drills.regression: Smaller arc, or swing only out to the side and back to the centre.

alternatives.why: Floor-based hip rotation if no support is free or you prefer slower control.
Where adductor flexibility is actually built: static holds after the session ([[dec:D27]]).

drills.whyChosen: Squats, lunges, running and martial-arts footwork all move the hip sideways as well as forwards. Side swings cover that plane in under a minute with no equipment (practical convention). See [[dec:D10]].
drills.safety: Hold the support with both hands, especially while standing on your weaker left leg. Stop with sharp groin pain; a gentle stretch is the target.
drills.mechanism: As with front-back swings, the short-term gain in [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] is mostly greater [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]] plus local warming, not a longer muscle [@Weppler2010_sensory_theory]. The standing leg works too: its hip abductors keep the pelvis level on one leg (background anatomy).
drills.evidence: Dynamic stretching gave about +1.3% in performance immediately afterwards, versus -3.7% for static stretching [@Behm2016_acute_stretching]. For acute ROM, stretching was no better than other warm-up activity (ES 0.01) [@Warneke2024_FR_stretch_warmup_ROM]. No trial has tested side swings specifically; the dose is practical convention.

drills.name: World's greatest stretch
equipment: 2 m of floor; a mat for the rear knee
drills.summary: A slow lunge sequence: step into a long lunge, drop the inside elbow towards the front instep, rotate and reach that arm to the ceiling, then optionally straighten the front knee. One drill moves the hip flexors, adductors, hamstrings and upper back, which suits your tight hamstrings and long hours at a desk.
drills.dose: 3 per side, left leg forward first, in the full-body A, lower-day, athletic lower-day and test-day warm-ups. Pause 2-3 s in each position; about 1.5 min in total.
setup: Stand tall with about 2 m of clear floor ahead.
Put a mat where the rear knee will land if the floor is hard.
execution: Step the left foot forward into a long lunge; lower the right knee to the floor or just above it.
Place the right hand on the floor inside the left foot and bring the left elbow down towards the left instep; hold 2-3 s.
Rotate the chest to the left and reach the left hand to the ceiling, eyes following the hand; hold 2-3 s.
Hamstring option: both hands down, shift the hips back and straighten the front knee as far as is comfortable, toes up; hold 2 s.
Step back to standing and repeat on the right side.
cues: Turn the chest; eyes follow the hand.

errors.error: A short stance, so the hips stay high and the rear hip flexor is not stretched.
errors.fix: Lengthen the step until the front of the rear hip feels a mild stretch as you sink.

errors.error: Rushing through the positions.
errors.fix: Pause 2-3 s in each; this is a mobility drill, not cardio.

errors.error: Forcing the straight-knee hamstring position by rounding the back.
errors.fix: Bend the front knee a little; your hamstrings set the limit.

drills.progression: Add the hamstring option on every rep, then make it a walking version that travels across the floor.
drills.regression: Rear knee down on a mat; elbow only to the inside of the knee; a smaller rotation.

alternatives.why: Thoracic rotation alone, lying down, if lunging is uncomfortable.
Static hip-flexor stretching after the session, part of the flexibility programme.

drills.whyChosen: One drill covers four areas, which keeps a warm-up you do alone short enough to do every time (practical convention). The lunge also rehearses the split-squat and lunge patterns you lift. See [[dec:D10]] and [[dec:D27]].
drills.safety: Stop with pinching at the front of the hip or pain in the lower back. In the hamstring option a stretch is expected; a sharp pull or tingling down the leg is not.
drills.mechanism: Holding each position for a few seconds under your own control warms the tissue and lets the nervous system accept more range; acute [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] gains are mostly greater [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]] [@Weppler2010_sensory_theory]. The holds stay far below the 60 s or more per muscle at which [[term:static-stretching|static stretching]] reliably reduces force [@Kay2012_acute_static_stretch].
drills.evidence: Within a full warm-up, short static stretches (60 s or less per muscle) impair strength and power only trivially, by about 1-2% [@Chaabene2019_static_stretching_review], and dynamic stretching gave about +1.3% [@Behm2016_acute_stretching]. The drill itself has not been tested in trials; its dose is practical convention.

drills.name: Bodyweight squat with pause (prying squat)
drills.system: squat pattern rehearsal / hip and ankle mobility
equipment: none; a rack upright to hold if needed
drills.summary: Slow bodyweight squats with a 2-3 s pause at the bottom, using the elbows to push the knees out ('prying'). They rehearse the squat pattern and open the hips and ankles before any loaded leg work.
drills.dose: 6 reps with a 2-3 s pause at the bottom in the full-body A, lower-day and athletic lower-day warm-ups. Not a working set: finish without any fatigue.
setup: Feet about shoulder-width, toes turned out 15-30 deg.
Hands together in front of the chest, as if holding a goblet.
execution: Sit down between your heels over 2-3 s, heels down and chest up.
At the bottom, place the elbows inside the knees and gently push the knees out; shift your weight side to side for 2-3 s.
Stand by pushing through the whole foot, knees tracking over the toes.
Squat only as deep as you can keep the heels down and the lower back from rounding.

errors.error: Heels lift at the bottom.
errors.fix: Widen the stance a little and turn the toes out more; [[ex:wu-ankle-rock]] helps over weeks.

errors.error: Lower back rounds at the bottom.
errors.fix: Stop just above the depth where it happens; depth comes with practice.

errors.error: Knees cave inwards on the way up.
errors.fix: Push the knees out in line with the toes throughout.

drills.progression: Hold a light dumbbell as a goblet squat, or extend the pause to 5 s.
drills.regression: Hold a rack upright, or squat to a bench.

alternatives.why: The loaded version; a light set can be your first ramp-up set.
Hip rotation on the floor if squatting is uncomfortable that day.

drills.whyChosen: Before loaded squats, lunges or leg press, unloaded rehearsal lets you find a depth you control while stiff hips settle (practical convention). The pause removes bounce, so you feel where your range really ends, which matters when no coach is watching.
drills.safety: Stop with sharp knee or hip pain; a mild stretch in the groin or calves is expected. Hold a support if you lose balance at the bottom.
drills.mechanism: Low-load repetitions warm the working muscles and rehearse the motor pattern; the prying shifts take the hips through abduction and external rotation under body weight (background physiology). Light repetitions alone prime performance little, which is why your [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]] still follow [@Ribeiro2020_specific_warmup_RT].
drills.evidence: In trained men, specific warm-ups reaching about 80% of the training load gave slightly higher bar velocity and work (ES 0.4-0.8) than a few light repetitions, which were judged insufficient [@Ribeiro2020_specific_warmup_RT]. Expert consensus supports a layered warm-up of general, specific and conditioning activities [@Boullosa2026_warmup_Delphi]. The prying squat itself is practical convention.

drills.name: Glute bridge
equipment: mat
drills.summary: Lying on your back with knees bent, you lift the hips until knees, hips and shoulders form a straight line, and squeeze for 1 s. A low-load hip-extension drill that warms the glutes before squats, hinges and jumps.
drills.dose: 10 reps with a 1 s squeeze at the top in the full-body B and athletic lower-day warm-ups.
setup: Lie on your back on a mat, knees bent about 90 deg, feet flat and hip-width apart.
Arms by your sides, palms down.
execution: Set a light [[term:bracing|brace]] and press through the heels to lift the hips.
Stop when knees, hips and shoulders form a straight line; squeeze the glutes for 1 s.
Lower over about 2 s, touch the floor lightly and repeat.

errors.error: Arching the lower back to lift higher.
errors.fix: Stop at the straight line and keep the ribs down; the work should be felt in the glutes, not the back.

errors.error: Hamstrings cramp or do most of the work.
errors.fix: Move the feet closer to the hips and push through the heels.

drills.progression: Single-leg bridge, left leg first, 6-8 per side; it also fits a pre-run hip-and-core routine.
drills.regression: Smaller range, or no pause at the top.

alternatives.why: The loaded version, used in the main session for glute growth.
Rehearses the squat pattern if floor space is scarce.

drills.whyChosen: Hip extension drives squats, Romanian deadlifts, jumps and running. A short bridge set warms it with almost no fatigue and without asking anything of your tight hamstrings' length (practical convention).
drills.safety: Low risk. Stop with lower-back pain and use a smaller range.
drills.mechanism: With the knees bent, the hamstrings work from a shortened position and contribute less, so the glutes do more of the hip extension (background biomechanics). Claims that bridges 'switch on' dormant glutes and so improve lifting are not tested in the sources here (inference); the drill is warming and rehearsal.
drills.evidence: No trial in these catalogues tests bridges as a warm-up drill; their use here is practical convention. A physiotherapist-supervised hip-and-core programme before runs reduced lower-limb injuries in adult novice runners compared with static stretching (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.45-0.97) [@Leppanen2024_RunRCT]; its exact exercises are not recorded in this programme's sources, so linking it to bridges is inference.

drills.name: Ankle rocks (knee-to-wall)
equipment: wall or rack upright
drills.summary: In a split stance facing a wall, you drive the front knee forward over the toes towards the wall with the heel down, then rock back. It mobilises dorsiflexion (the shin moving forward over the foot), which squats, lunges and running all need.
drills.dose: 10 per side, left first, heel down, in the full-body B, cardio and run warm-ups.
setup: Face a wall in a short split stance, front foot 5-10 cm from the wall, hands on the wall.
Left foot in front first; the front heel stays down throughout.
execution: Drive the left knee forward towards the wall, in line with the second or third toe, until the calf feels a stretch or the heel is about to lift.
Hold 1-2 s, then rock back.
Repeat 10 times, then switch legs.
Move the foot further from the wall as range improves.

errors.error: Heel lifts as the knee goes forward.
errors.fix: Move the foot closer to the wall; the heel staying down is the whole point.

errors.error: Knee collapses inwards to reach the wall.
errors.fix: Aim the knee over the second or third toe.

errors.error: Pinching at the front of the ankle.
errors.fix: Reduce the range; if it persists, follow [[rule:pain]].

drills.progression: Move the foot further from the wall over the weeks; add a 2 s hold at end range.
drills.regression: Smaller rocks with both hands on a rack for support.

alternatives.why: Static calf stretching after the session builds lasting dorsiflexion range.
Loads dorsiflexion in the bottom of a squat.

drills.whyChosen: Limited dorsiflexion makes the heels lift and the trunk tip forward in squats and lunges (practical convention). The position is the same as your [[ex:test-knee-wall|knee-to-wall test]], so the drill doubles as a quick self-check.
drills.safety: Stop with sharp pain at the front of the ankle or in the Achilles. Once running and jumping begin, treat Achilles soreness that lasts into the next day as a reason to hold progression (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: Short-term gains come mainly from warmth and greater [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]] [@Weppler2010_sensory_theory]. Lasting gains need repeated stretching: in one trial a calf-stretching programme increased dorsiflexion by 7.3 deg (95% CI 4.1-10.5) and lowered muscle stiffness [@Andrade2020_muscle_nerve_stretching].
drills.evidence: The knee-to-wall measurement is reliable when clinicians take it (ICC 0.65-0.99), with a minimal detectable change of about 1.6-1.9 cm or 4.6-4.7 deg [@Powden2015_WBLT_reliability], so changes under about 2 cm are noise. Four weeks of high-discomfort calf stretching (6-7/10) raised dorsiflexion by 40%, versus 15% at low discomfort [@Nakamura2021_HI_vs_LI_SS]; gentle warm-up rocks are not meant to do that. The dose is practical convention.

drills.name: Cat-camel
equipment: mat
drills.summary: On hands and knees, you slowly round the whole back towards the ceiling, then let it sag, staying within a comfortable range. An unloaded way to move the spine through flexion and extension before lifting.
drills.dose: 8 slow cycles (about 4 s each) in the full-body A warm-up.
setup: Hands under the shoulders, knees under the hips, on a mat.
Neck relaxed, eyes on the floor.
execution: Breathe out and slowly round the whole back up, tucking the chin and the tailbone.
Breathe in and slowly let the back sag, lifting the chest and tailbone.
Use about three-quarters of your range; stop short of strain at either end.
Move continuously without holding the end positions.
cues: Slow wave from tail to head.

errors.error: Forcing the end range in either direction.
errors.fix: Stay at about three-quarters of your range; the aim is motion, not stretch.

errors.error: Moving only the neck or only the lower back.
errors.fix: Let each part of the spine move in turn, from pelvis to head.

drills.progression: None needed; keep it a gentle motion drill.
drills.regression: Smaller range, or round and arch while seated on a bench.

alternatives.why: Thoracic rotation rather than flexion-extension.
Combines spinal rotation with hip mobility if time is short.

drills.whyChosen: You train about an hour after waking. Intervertebral discs take up water during a night lying down, and coaches commonly avoid loaded end-range spinal bending in the first hour after rising, using gentle unloaded motion like this instead (practical convention; not tested in this programme's sources). It also suits a body that sits at a desk for about 9 hours a day.
drills.safety: Stop with pain that spreads into a leg, or with numbness or tingling, and follow [[rule:pain]].
drills.mechanism: Slow cyclic motion warms the trunk tissues and moves each spinal segment through part of its range without load (background physiology). It will not fix your toe-touch: fingertip-to-floor distance tracks how far the whole trunk flexes (r -0.96 with radiographic trunk flexion in a small sample of patients with back pain) [@Perret2001_fingertip_floor_test], and changing that is the job of the flexibility programme, not a warm-up drill (inference).
drills.evidence: No trial in these catalogues tests the cat-camel; its use is practical convention. What is supported is the general principle: warm-ups improved performance in 79% of the outcomes studied, with little sign of harm [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance].

drills.name: Thoracic open book
equipment: mat; optional rolled towel between the knees
drills.summary: Lying on your side with hips and knees bent to 90 deg, you sweep the top arm open like the cover of a book, rotating the upper back while the knees stay stacked. It restores upper-back rotation before pressing and pulling.
drills.dose: 6 per side in the upper-day warm-up, with a 2 s pause in the open position. Lie on your right side first, so the left arm opens first.
setup: Lie on your right side, hips and knees bent about 90 deg, knees stacked.
Arms straight out in front at shoulder height, palms together.
Optional: a rolled towel between the knees keeps them stacked.
execution: Keeping the knees together and on the floor, lift the top (left) arm and sweep it up and over, eyes following the hand.
Rotate until the upper back stops turning, the arm reaching towards the floor behind you; pause 2 s and breathe out.
Return the arm to the start.
Do 6, then turn over.
cues: Turn the chest, not just the arm.

errors.error: Knees lift or slide apart, so the rotation comes from the lower back.
errors.fix: Press the top knee into the floor or the towel.

errors.error: Forcing the arm to the floor with a pinch at the front of the shoulder.
errors.fix: Bend the elbow and stop where the chest stops turning.

drills.progression: Hold the open position for 2 slow breaths, or progress to rotations on hands and knees with one hand behind the head (practical convention).
drills.regression: A smaller arc with the elbow bent.

alternatives.why: Thoracic rotation combined with a lunge.
Shoulder range overhead rather than rotation.

drills.whyChosen: Long hours at a desk tend to leave the upper back stiff into rotation and extension, and upper-back motion helps you keep the shoulder blades set on bench and overhead presses (practical convention). Lying on your side locks the lower back, so the movement comes from where you want it.
drills.safety: Stop with shoulder pain or pins and needles in the hand; tingling usually means the arm is too straight and too far back, so bend the elbow.
drills.mechanism: Bent hips lock the lumbar spine, concentrating rotation in the thoracic segments, whose joint orientation allows more rotation than the lumbar spine does (background anatomy). Short-term range gains are mostly warmth and greater [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]] [@Weppler2010_sensory_theory].
drills.evidence: No trial in these catalogues tests the open book; its use and dose are practical convention. In upper-body warm-up research, high-load dynamic warm-ups enhanced strength and power while short static stretching had no effect on power [@McCrary2015_upperbody_warmup], so the [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]] that follow do the performance work and this drill prepares range.

drills.name: Band pull-apart
equipment: light resistance band; if none, a light cable at shoulder height
drills.summary: Holding a light band at shoulder height with straight arms, you pull it apart until it touches the chest, squeezing the shoulder blades together. It warms the upper back and rear shoulders before pressing and pulling.
drills.dose: 15 reps with a light band in the full-body B and upper-day warm-ups, at about [[term:rpe|rating of perceived exertion (RPE)]] 3-4; never close to failure.
setup: Stand tall, band at shoulder height, hands about shoulder-width apart, palms down.
Arms straight, elbows soft.
execution: Pull the band apart by moving the hands out to the sides until it touches the chest.
Squeeze the shoulder blades back and down for 1 s.
Return over about 2 s, keeping tension in the band.

errors.error: Shrugging the shoulders towards the ears.
errors.fix: Use a lighter band and think of tucking the shoulder blades into your back pockets.

errors.error: Arching the lower back to finish the rep.
errors.fix: Keep the ribs down; use a lighter band.

errors.error: Band so stiff that the elbows bend.
errors.fix: Choose a band you can pull apart 15 times smoothly with straight arms.

drills.progression: Vary the grip (palms up, or diagonal pulls) rather than adding resistance; the warm-up should not tire you.
drills.regression: Wider grip or a lighter band.

alternatives.why: Cable version, also a main-session rear-delt exercise.
Machine option for rear delts as a working exercise.

drills.whyChosen: It rehearses holding the shoulder blades back, the position for bench presses and rows, and adds a little rear-shoulder work to balance the pressing in your programme (practical convention). It needs only a band, so it works on a crowded gym floor. See [[dec:D10]].
drills.safety: Check the band for nicks or tears first; a snapping band can hit the face. Stop with pain at the front of the shoulder.
drills.mechanism: Light sets raise local muscle temperature and rehearse scapular retraction and depression (background physiology). The load is far below what produces post-activation performance enhancement, so the drill prepares and rehearses rather than potentiates (inference).
drills.evidence: High-load dynamic warm-ups enhanced upper-body strength and power, and passive heating was largely ineffective [@McCrary2015_upperbody_warmup]; a light band is not that stimulus, so this drill and its 15-rep dose are practical convention. Your [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]] provide the high-load part.

drills.name: Band or stick pass-through (shoulder dislocate)
equipment: light long band, PVC pipe, dowel or broomstick
drills.summary: With a wide grip on a band or stick, you raise it overhead with straight arms, carry it down behind your back and return. Despite the nickname nothing is dislocated: it is a controlled shoulder-range drill before pressing and pulling.
drills.dose: 8-10 reps in the upper-day warm-up, wide grip, pain-free range only.
setup: Hold the band or stick in front of the thighs with a wide grip, palms down.
Stand tall with the ribs down.
execution: With straight arms, raise the band in front of you and overhead.
Continue back until it touches the lower back or buttocks, if your range allows.
Return the same way, about 2 s each direction.
Narrow the grip slightly only when the whole arc is easy.

errors.error: Grip too narrow, so the elbows bend or the shoulder pinches.
errors.fix: Widen the grip until the whole arc is smooth and painless.

errors.error: Arching the lower back to get the band behind you.
errors.fix: Brace and stop where the back starts to arch.

errors.error: One arm leading (usually the tighter side).
errors.fix: Slow down and keep the band level.

drills.progression: Narrow the grip by 1-2 cm every few weeks, as long as the arc stays painless.
drills.regression: Half arc (to overhead and back), or a more elastic band.

alternatives.why: Upper-back rotation if overhead range is irritable.
Static lat stretching after the session if overhead range is limited.

drills.whyChosen: Overhead pressing, pulldowns and pull-ups need the arms to reach overhead without the lower back arching. A band is forgiving: when your range runs out it stretches instead of forcing the shoulder, which suits training with no one watching your form (practical convention).
drills.safety: Never force the end of the arc. Stop with pain, painful clicking or a feeling of instability at the front of the shoulder, and widen the grip.
drills.mechanism: The arc takes the shoulder through full flexion and extension, lengthening the lats, pectorals and front of the shoulder in turn; short-term gains in [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] reflect warmth and greater [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]] [@Weppler2010_sensory_theory].
drills.evidence: No trial in these catalogues tests pass-throughs; drill and dose are practical convention. For acute ROM, stretching drills were no better than other warm-up activity (ES 0.01) [@Warneke2024_FR_stretch_warmup_ROM], so the main value here is rehearsing the overhead position (inference).

drills.name: Scapular push-up
equipment: none; a bench for the easier version
drills.summary: In a push-up position with straight arms, you let the chest sink between the shoulder blades, then push the floor away to spread them, without bending the elbows. It warms the serratus anterior, which holds the shoulder blade against the ribcage during pushing and overhead work.
drills.dose: 10 slow reps with a 1 s pause at each end in the full-body B, upper-day and test-day warm-ups.
setup: High plank: hands under the shoulders, arms straight, body in a straight line.
If a full plank is hard, put your knees down or your hands on a bench.
execution: Keeping the elbows straight, let the chest sink so the shoulder blades move together.
Push the floor away so the shoulder blades spread apart and the upper back rounds slightly.
Pause 1 s at each end; keep the hips level throughout.

errors.error: Bending the elbows, turning it into a small push-up.
errors.fix: Lock the elbows; all motion happens at the shoulder blades.

errors.error: Hips sagging or piking.
errors.fix: Squeeze the glutes to keep a straight line, or drop to the knees.

errors.error: A tiny range.
errors.fix: Move slowly to both ends; the range is only a few centimetres, but use all of it.

drills.progression: Add a 2 s hold in the pushed-away position; later, a plank with alternating shoulder taps.
drills.regression: Hands on a bench or knees on the floor.

alternatives.why: Finishing each push-up with a full push-away trains the same action under load.
A plank held in the pushed-away position is a static version.

drills.whyChosen: With a baseline of 5 push-ups you will spend many weeks in the push-up position, and this drill rehearses the shoulder-blade control those reps need at almost no fatigue cost (practical convention). On test days it comes before the [[ex:test-pushup|push-up test]].
drills.safety: Stop with wrist or shoulder pain; if the wrists ache, use fists, push-up handles or dumbbell handles.
drills.mechanism: The serratus anterior protracts and upwardly rotates the scapula and keeps it flat on the ribcage; weakness or poor timing is classically linked with a 'winging' shoulder blade (background anatomy). With the arm fixed, the drill isolates scapular motion, rehearsing that control before loaded pressing (inference).
drills.evidence: No trial in these catalogues tests scapular push-ups as a warm-up; drill and dose are practical convention. Warm-ups in general improved performance in 79% of measured outcomes [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance], and high-load dynamic warm-ups enhanced upper-body strength and power [@McCrary2015_upperbody_warmup], a job your [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]] do rather than this drill.

drills.name: 90/90 hip switches
equipment: mat
drills.summary: Sitting on the floor with both knees bent to 90 deg, one leg in front of you and one to the side, you rotate both knees over to the other side so the legs swap roles. It moves both hips through internal and external rotation, a range that squats, lunges and martial-arts stances use and desk sitting rarely does.
drills.dose: 5 per side (10 switches) in the lower-day warm-up, slowly, about 3 s per switch.
setup: Sit on a mat, knees bent about 90 deg, feet a little wider than hip-width.
Hands on the floor behind you for support.
execution: Let both knees fall to the left, so the left leg lies in front of you (external rotation) and the right leg to the side (internal rotation).
Pause 1-2 s, sitting as tall as you comfortably can.
Lift both knees and rotate them to the right to switch sides.
Keep the feet planted and move from the hips.
cues: Sit tall, chest over the front shin.

errors.error: Slumping back and using the hands to force the knees down.
errors.fix: Keep hand support light and move only as far as the hips allow.

errors.error: Pain on the inside of the rear (internally rotated) knee.
errors.fix: Widen the feet or reduce how far the knees drop; the knee should not twist.

drills.progression: Take the hands off the floor; then lean the chest over the front shin for 2 s on each side.
drills.regression: Hands behind you, wider feet, or sit on a folded mat or low step.

alternatives.why: Standing hip mobility if floor work is inconvenient.
Static external-rotation stretch for after the session.

drills.whyChosen: Hip rotation is usually missing from a front-back warm-up, yet deep squats, lunges and the stances of any martial art you take up need it (practical convention). The switches are slow and active, so they combine range with control.
drills.safety: Stop with pinching at the front of the hip, groin pain or knee pain; reduce the range or widen the feet.
drills.mechanism: Moving actively into internal and external rotation warms the deep hip rotators and joint capsule and practises control near end range; acute gains in [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] are mostly warmth and greater [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]] [@Weppler2010_sensory_theory]. Moving under your own muscle power keeps the drill close to [[term:dynamic-stretching|dynamic stretching]], which did not impair performance [@Behm2016_acute_stretching].
drills.evidence: No trial in these catalogues tests 90/90 switches; drill and dose are practical convention. For acute ROM, stretching was no better than other warm-up activity (ES 0.01) [@Warneke2024_FR_stretch_warmup_ROM], so the choice of drill matters less than doing some active preparation (inference).

drills.name: Pick-ups (short accelerations)

primary: heart rate and breathing at interval intensity
secondary: working legs (and arms on the rower)

equipment: the bike, rower or treadmill you will use for the intervals
drills.summary: Two short bursts at the intensity of the coming intervals, with easy work between, at the end of the interval-day warm-up. Heart rate, breathing and legs meet the target effort briefly, so the first real interval is not a shock, and you rehearse the pace.
drills.dose: 2 x 20 s at interval effort with 40 s easy between, after the 8 min easy-to-moderate warm-up on interval days. Then 1-2 min easy before interval 1.
setup: Use the same machine and settings you will use for the intervals.
Decide the target speed, resistance or watts before you start.
execution: After the 8 min warm-up, raise the effort to the planned interval intensity over 3-5 s.
Hold it for 20 s and note how it feels.
Drop to easy for 40 s, then repeat once.
Go easy for 1-2 min, then start interval 1.
cues: Find the pace, don't race it.

errors.error: Going harder than the interval target.
errors.fix: Match, don't exceed, the planned intensity; pick-ups are a rehearsal.

errors.error: Starting the intervals straight after the second pick-up.
errors.fix: Take 1-2 min easy first so breathing settles.

drills.progression: None needed; when the interval target changes, match the pick-ups to it.
drills.regression: One pick-up instead of two, or 15 s each.

alternatives.why: The general warm-up that comes first; pick-ups add the specific layer.
The equivalent preparation before runs.

drills.whyChosen: Brief efforts close to the main task form the specific layer of the expert-consensus warm-up model [@Boullosa2026_warmup_Delphi]. For [[term:hiit|high-intensity interval training (HIIT)]] done alone they double as a pacing check: if 20 s at target already feels hard, start the intervals slightly easier (practical convention). See [[dec:D13]].
drills.safety: If a pick-up brings chest pain, dizziness, palpitations or unusual breathlessness, stop and follow [[plan:safety]]. On a day when moderate effort already feels hard, do easy cardio instead of intervals (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: Short near-target efforts speed up the oxygen-uptake response of the work that follows and recruit the higher-threshold [[term:motor-unit|motor units]] the intervals will use (background physiology, not measured in the cited sources). Any post-activation effect is short-lived, so the main value is readiness and pacing (inference).
drills.evidence: Expert consensus (low certainty) describes warm-ups as general, specific and conditioning layers, with more comprehensive warm-ups judged more effective [@Boullosa2026_warmup_Delphi]. Warm-ups in general improved performance in 79% of measured outcomes [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance]. The 2 x 20 s dose is practical convention.

drills.name: Jump rope (easy)
equipment: speed or beaded rope adjusted to your height
firm, non-slip floor (rubber or wood)
drills.summary: Easy two-foot skipping at a relaxed rhythm. From [[phase:p2]] it can replace the last part of the easy cardio warm-up, adding rhythm, footwork and gentle, repeated ankle loading.
drills.dose: From [[phase:p2]]: 2 x 30-60 s easy, at the end of the general warm-up. It is not in a fixed warm-up block, so use it as a swap. Dose it by time, not by jumps, and keep it out of your plyometric contact count.
setup: Rope length: standing on the middle, the handles reach about armpit height.
Find a clear space away from mirrors, racks and walkways.
execution: Hold the handles at hip height, elbows close to the body; turn the rope with the wrists.
Bounce on the balls of the feet, 2-5 cm off the floor, knees soft.
Keep a steady, easy rhythm; after a trip, just restart.
Once two-foot bouncing is smooth, try alternate feet or side-to-side.

errors.error: Jumping high and landing heavily.
errors.fix: Clear the rope by only a few centimetres and aim to be quiet.

errors.error: Turning the rope with the whole arm.
errors.fix: Elbows in; the wrists do the work.

errors.error: Doing too much early, leaving the calves sore.
errors.fix: Stay at 2 x 30-60 s for the first weeks; add time only if the calves feel normal the next day.

drills.progression: About 1 extra minute of total skipping per week, then alternate-foot, side-to-side and crossover patterns (inference).
drills.regression: Shadow skipping without the rope, or 15-20 s bouts.

alternatives.why: The default general warm-up on a machine.
Footwork rhythm without repeated bouncing.

drills.whyChosen: It is cheap, quick and adds rhythm and footwork variety that suits your interest in martial arts and dance, which helps against boredom (practical convention). It waits until [[phase:p2]] so the calves and Achilles first adapt to lifting and walking: the collagen of the adult Achilles tendon core is essentially not renewed [@Heinemeier2013_tendon14C], one reason tendon is thought to adapt more slowly than muscle (inference).
drills.safety: Hold progression if calf or Achilles soreness lasts beyond 24 h, and skip it on days with Achilles pain. Avoid bare concrete (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: Skipping is a low-amplitude, high-repetition [[term:ssc|stretch-shortening cycle]] activity: the calf-Achilles spring is pre-activated, loaded and recoils on every contact [@Nicol2006_SSC]. The contacts are submaximal, so they are not equivalent to plyometric jumps and are dosed by time (inference).
drills.evidence: Jump-rope training for 6-40 weeks improved cardiorespiratory endurance, jumping, sprinting, strength and fat mass versus controls (ES 0.23-1.19), but not lean mass or bone [@Singh2022_jumprope]. In 18 of the 21 studies the mean age was under 18, so this is indirect for you; no adult dose or safety data were found.

drills.name: Running drills (A-skip, carioca, high knees)
equipment: about 15 m of clear floor, track or quiet path
drills.summary: Short rhythmic drills that exaggerate parts of the running stride: A-skips (a skip with a high knee and an active foot strike), high knees (quick, small knee lifts) and carioca (a sideways grapevine). Used before runs, and carioca before agility work, from [[phase:p2]].
drills.dose: Before runs: A-skip and high knees, 2 x 15 m each, walking back as recovery, after the brisk walk, leg swings and ankle rocks. Carioca, 2 x 15 m each way, before change-of-direction work.
setup: Mark out about 15 m; in a crowded gym use a turf strip, a corridor or the space beside the studio.
Running shoes on.
execution: A-skip: skip forward, driving one knee to hip height while the other foot strikes the ground under the hip; the opposite arm swings. Rhythm before speed.
High knees: quick, small steps lifting the knees towards hip height on the balls of the feet, travelling forward slowly.
Carioca: move sideways, the trailing leg crossing alternately in front of and behind the lead leg, hips rotating; lead with the left first, then the right.
Walk back to the start between reps.

errors.error: Leaning back and reaching the foot out in front.
errors.fix: Stay tall with a slight forward lean and land under the hip.

errors.error: Going fast before the rhythm is smooth.
errors.fix: Slow down; these are coordination drills.

errors.error: Arms crossing the body.
errors.fix: Swing the arms forward and back with the elbows at about 90 deg.

drills.progression: Slightly more speed once the rhythm is smooth; later add B-skips, which extend the leg after the knee lift (practical convention).
drills.regression: Marching versions (A-march, high-knee march) at walking pace.

alternatives.why: Short accelerations on machine interval days.
Footwork rhythm in place if there is no 15 m strip.

drills.whyChosen: They rehearse rhythm, posture and foot placement just before running and raise the heart rate further without much fatigue (practical convention). Transfer from generic drills to other skills is unproven, so treat them as preparation for the run that follows rather than a separate coordination goal. See [[dec:D14]].
drills.safety: Keep the amplitude low on hard or uneven surfaces. Stop with calf, Achilles or shin pain and follow [[rule:running]] and [[rule:pain]].
drills.mechanism: The drills rehearse the [[term:ssc|stretch-shortening cycle]] of running at low intensity: the leg is pre-activated before ground contact and loaded briefly [@Nicol2006_SSC]. Skill learned this way is expected to stay largely specific to the drill, by analogy with balance and change-of-direction training [@Kummel2016_specificity; @NygaardFalch2019_COD] (inference).
drills.evidence: No trial in these catalogues tests running drills; their use is practical convention. The best-supported pre-run routine is a supervised hip-and-core programme, which reduced lower-limb injuries in adult novice runners versus static stretching (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.45-0.97) [@Leppanen2024_RunRCT].

drills.name: Single-leg stance (balance practice)

primary: ankle and hip stabilisers of the standing leg

equipment: wall or rack upright within arm's reach
later: foam pad or folded mat
drills.summary: Standing on one leg for 30 s, left leg first, progressing from eyes open to head turns, eyes closed and a soft surface. It is the core of your balance work, because your left leg balances worse than your right (20 vs 30 s eyes open, 10 vs 15 s eyes closed).
drills.dose: 2 x 30 s per leg, left first, in the full-body A, full-body B, upper-day and lower-day warm-ups; on upper and lower days, progress to eyes closed. If you touch down, reset and continue until 30 s of standing is accumulated.
setup: Stand barefoot or in flat shoes beside a wall or rack, close enough to touch it.
Arms crossed on the chest, as in the test, or relaxed; eyes on a fixed point at eye level.
execution: Lift the right foot so you stand on the left first; keep the raised foot near, but not touching, the standing ankle.
Hold 30 s with a soft standing knee; small ankle wobbles are the training stimulus.
Switch legs, then repeat both for a second round.
Progress in this order: eyes open, slow head turns, eyes closed, foam pad.
cues: Spread the toes; whole foot on the floor.

errors.error: Resting the raised foot against the standing leg.
errors.fix: Keep it near the ankle without contact.

errors.error: Leaning on the wall.
errors.fix: Hover a hand near it and touch only to catch yourself.

errors.error: Locking the standing knee.
errors.fix: Keep it slightly bent so the ankle and hip do the balancing.

drills.progression: When 2 x 30 s is steady, move to the next step: head turns, then eyes closed, then a foam pad. Add difficulty rather than holding beyond about 40 s.
drills.regression: A fingertip on the wall, or 15-20 s bouts accumulated to 30 s.

alternatives.why: Dynamic balance with reaching, from [[phase:p2]].
Loaded single-leg balance that also trains the hamstrings.
The standardised version used to re-check the asymmetry.

drills.whyChosen: Healthy people's dominant and non-dominant legs balance equally on average [@Schorderet2021_dominance], so a one-third left-side gap is probably unusual (inference); going left first gives the weaker leg your freshest attention. Gains are largely specific to the task practised [@Kummel2016_specificity], so practising stance should improve stance, and the harder variations move it towards real demands. See [[dec:D28]].
drills.safety: Always stand within reach of a wall or rack, especially with eyes closed: you train alone and a fall in a busy gym is the main risk. Stop if you feel dizzy.
drills.mechanism: Balance training produces [[term:neural-adaptation|neural adaptations]] at spinal (reflex) and supraspinal levels, shown with H-reflex, magnetic-stimulation and imaging methods [@Taube2008_balancemech]. Closing the eyes forces reliance on [[term:proprioception|proprioception]] and the vestibular system, which is why eyes-closed times are much shorter (background physiology).
drills.evidence: In healthy young adults, balance training improved steady-state balance (ES 0.73; 0.82 in untrained people), best with about 11-12 weeks, 3 sessions/week, 2 sets and 21-40 s bouts [@Lesinski2015_balanceDR]. Proprioception training reduced sports injuries (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.35-0.87), mostly in team sports [@Lauersen2014_injury_prevention]. Under the standard protocol, men aged 18-39 average about 44 s eyes open and 17 s best-of-3 eyes closed, with very wide spread for eyes closed [@Springer2007_unipedalstance].

drills.name: Single-leg reach (star excursion)

primary: ankle, knee and hip control of the standing leg
secondary: glutes and quadriceps of the standing leg

equipment: three tape lines on the floor in a Y or star (optional)
wall nearby
drills.summary: Standing on one leg, you reach the other foot as far as you can control forward, to the side and back, tapping the floor lightly with the toe and returning without putting weight on it. It turns static balance into controlled single-leg squatting in several directions, closer to running, hiking and martial-arts footwork.
drills.dose: From [[phase:p2]], in the athletic lower-day warm-up: 2 rounds x 3 reaches (forward, side, back) per leg, standing on the left leg first.
setup: Stand on the left leg at the centre of the tape lines, hands on hips, near a wall.
Standing foot flat, toes pointing forward.
execution: Bend the standing knee and hip and reach the right foot forward as far as you can control; tap the floor lightly with the toe.
Return to the centre without putting weight on the reaching foot.
Repeat to the side and then behind, diagonally past the standing heel.
That is one round; do two, then switch legs.

errors.error: Putting weight on the reaching foot.
errors.fix: Shorten the reach; the tap should be feather-light.

errors.error: Standing knee collapsing inwards.
errors.fix: Keep the knee over the second toe and reduce the depth.

errors.error: Heel of the standing foot lifting.
errors.fix: Reach less far and keep the whole foot down.

drills.progression: Reach further; add directions up to the full 8-point star; hold the furthest point for 2 s; later hold light dumbbells.
drills.regression: Shorter reaches, a fingertip on the wall, or fewer directions.

alternatives.why: Static single-leg stance if dynamic reaching is too hard.
A loaded version of the backward reach that also trains the hamstrings.

drills.whyChosen: Balance gains are largely specific to what is practised [@Kummel2016_specificity], so moving balance should resemble the single-leg landings and pivots of running, hiking and martial arts better than standing still does (inference). Starting on the left keeps the focus on your weaker side. See [[dec:D28]].
drills.safety: Stay near a wall. Stop with knee pain in the standing leg and reduce the depth.
drills.mechanism: Each reach demands a controlled single-leg squat while the body's centre of mass moves towards the edge of the base of support, combining [[term:proprioception|proprioception]], hip and knee strength and anticipatory (proactive) balance control (background biomechanics).
drills.evidence: On Y-balance and star-excursion tests, dominant and non-dominant legs perform alike (SMD 0.06, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.16) [@Schorderet2021_dominance], so a persistent side difference is worth attention. Balance training improved proactive balance by ES 0.92 in young adults [@Lesinski2015_balanceDR]. The 3-reach dose is practical convention.

drills.name: Supine hamstring stretch (strap)
equipment: strap, towel or band
mat
drills.summary: Your main tool for the toe-touch limitation: a [[term:static-stretching|static stretch]] done lying down, so balance and the lower back are out of the picture and you can hold a precise, strong intensity. It is there for [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]], not recovery.
drills.dose: Full-body A, upper and lower cool-downs: 2 × 30 s per leg, left first, at about 7/10 (10 = the most you could tolerate). With a hamstring stretch in every cool-down, five sessions a week give about 5 min per leg.
setup: Lie on a mat, right knee bent with the foot flat (or that leg straight on the floor for more stretch).
Loop the strap round the ball of the left foot, one end in each hand.
execution: With the knee straight, draw the leg up until the back of the thigh reaches about 7/10.
Breathe slowly; as the tension eases after 10-15 s, draw the leg a little higher.
After 30 s switch legs, then repeat the round.

errors.error: Pelvis or lower back lifting off the mat
errors.fix: Lower the leg until the pelvis stays down; feel it in the thigh, not the back.

errors.error: Settling at a comfortable 3-4/10
errors.fix: Intensity mattered in one calf-stretching trial; hold a strong 7/10 you can breathe through.

drills.progression: 3 × 45 s per leg, or strap self-[[term:pnf|PNF]]: press the heel into the strap moderately for about 5 s, relax, draw the leg higher; 3-4 cycles. Retest with [[ex:test-ftf]] every 4-6 weeks at the same point in a session.
drills.regression: Unlock the knee slightly, or rest the straight leg against a rack upright instead of pulling.

alternatives.why: Standing version when floor space is short.
Loaded full-range hinge; resistance training improved ROM about as much as stretching.

drills.whyChosen: No balance demand (your left leg balances worse), fine control of intensity, and the strap makes it passive, which beat active static stretching for flexibility ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.97 vs 0.59) [@Arntz2023_chronic_SS_strength]. Training alone, the strap replaces a PNF partner.
drills.safety: Stop for sharp pain, or tingling, numbness or pain running down the leg: nerve tissue, not muscle, can limit the range [@Andrade2020_muscle_nerve_stretching]. Unlock the knee, stop pulling the toes back, and see [[rule:pain]].
drills.mechanism: Early gains are mostly [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]]: in a small study (n = 7), after 3 weeks of hamstring stretching people tolerated more angle and torque while muscle stiffness was unchanged [@Magnusson1996_stretch_tolerance]. Chronic stretching also lowered muscle stiffness modestly (ES -0.38), more with long, supervised static stretching [@Warneke2024_recalc_passive_properties].
drills.evidence: Stretch training increased ROM by an effect size of about 1.0 (95% CI 0.84-1.17) [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM]. In a 4-week [[term:rct|RCT]] of calf stretching in young men, stretching at 6-7/10 raised ROM by 40% versus 15% at 0-1/10 [@Nakamura2021_HI_vs_LI_SS]. In one review, at least about 5 min per week and more frequent sessions were linked to larger gains [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM], although a larger meta-analysis found no clear effect of dose or intensity [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM]; gains partly fade 2-6 weeks after stopping [@Konrad2025_detraining_ROM]. Post-exercise stretching did not reduce soreness in trials (very low certainty) [@Afonso2021_postexercise_stretch_recovery]. See [[dec:D27]].

drills.name: Standing hamstring stretch (heel on bench)
equipment: low bench or step
rack upright or wall to hold
drills.summary: A standing [[term:static-stretching|static stretch]] for the hamstrings that needs no floor space. The lean is a [[term:hip-hinge|hip hinge]], so it doubles as Romanian-deadlift practice. It alternates with the strap version so that every cool-down includes a hamstring stretch.
drills.dose: Full-body B and cardio cool-downs: 2 × 30 s per leg, left first, at about 7/10.
setup: Face a low bench beside a rack upright or wall you can hold.
Left heel on the bench, knee straight but not locked, toes up, hips square.
execution: Hinge forward from the hips with a long spine until the back of the thigh reaches about 7/10.
Hold 30 s, hinging slightly further as the tension eases.
Switch legs, holding the support now that you stand on your left leg, then repeat the round.

errors.error: Rounding the back to reach for the toes
errors.fix: Hands on the thigh, spine long, hinge at the hips; reaching moves the stretch into the back (practical convention).

errors.error: Bench so high that the pelvis tilts
errors.fix: Use a lower step; the stretch should arrive after a small hinge.

drills.progression: Hinge deeper at the same 7/10, hold 45-60 s, or add self-[[term:pnf|PNF]]: press the heel into the bench for about 5 s, relax, hinge further.
drills.regression: Lower step, slightly unlocked knee, or [[ex:st-ham-supine]] if balance or the back interferes.

alternatives.why: No balance demand and finer control of intensity.
Loaded single-leg hinge to long hamstring lengths, plus balance work.

drills.whyChosen: It works where floor space is scarce in a busy gym and adds variety (practical convention). It keeps hamstring stretching in every session, building the weekly time linked to larger gains in one review [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM].
drills.safety: Hold the support whenever you stand on the left leg. Stop for sharp pain or tingling down the leg and ease off; never bounce.
drills.mechanism: Three of the four hamstring muscles cross both hip and knee, so a hip hinge with a straight knee lengthens them at both ends. Early [[term:rom|ROM]] gains come mainly from [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]], not a longer muscle [@Weppler2010_sensory_theory].
drills.evidence: In a calf-stretching trial, stretching at 6-7/10 beat gentle stretching (40% vs 15% ROM gain in 4 weeks) [@Nakamura2021_HI_vs_LI_SS]. Resistance training raised ROM about as much as stretching, more in untrained people (ES 1.04), although lifting plus stretching gained no more than stretching alone [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM]; your Romanian deadlifts train this range too (inference). Track progress with [[ex:test-ftf]], which tracked radiographic trunk flexion closely in back-pain patients (r -0.96) [@Perret2001_fingertip_floor_test].

drills.name: Half-kneeling hip-flexor stretch
equipment: mat or folded towel for the knee
drills.summary: A [[term:static-stretching|static stretch]] for the front of the hip, which stays flexed through your 16:00-01:00 desk shift. The work is in the pelvis: tuck it under first, then shift forward only a little.
drills.dose: Full-body A and lower cool-downs: 2 × 30 s per side, left side first (left knee down).
setup: Kneel on the left knee on a pad, right foot forward, both knees at about 90°.
Tuck the pelvis under (tailbone down, belt buckle up) and squeeze the left glute.
execution: Keeping the tuck, shift the hips forward 2-5 cm until the front of the left hip stretches at about 6-7/10.
Stay tall with the ribs down for 30 s; switch sides, then repeat the round.

errors.error: Arching the lower back and lunging far forward
errors.fix: Back off the shift and re-tuck; a small movement with the tuck is the whole stretch.

errors.error: Kneeling on bare floor
errors.fix: Pad the knee with a mat or folded towel.

drills.progression: Raise the arm on the kneeling side and lean slightly away from it, or rest the back foot on a bench to bring in more rectus femoris.
drills.regression: Do it standing in a split stance with the back knee slightly bent, keeping the tuck.

alternatives.why: Dynamic version with a thoracic rotation; suits warm-ups.
Covers rectus femoris if kneeling is uncomfortable.

drills.whyChosen: Chosen for your working posture rather than a measured deficit: long sitting keeps the hip flexed, and keeping hip-extension range is a reasonable aim (inference; no hip-flexor trial is in our sources). The kneeling position lets you control the pelvis without a partner.
drills.safety: Pad the knee. Ease off for pinching at the front of the hip or pain in the lower back.
drills.mechanism: Tucking the pelvis (posterior tilt) moves the hip flexors' pelvic attachments away from the thigh, so a small forward shift is enough to stretch them (anatomy). Rectus femoris also crosses the knee, which is why raising the back foot increases its share.
drills.evidence: No hip-flexor-specific study is in our catalogues. Stretch training in general increased [[term:rom|ROM]] by an effect size of about 1.0 [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM], and about 60 s per exercise on at least 2 days a week is the consensus recommendation [@Garber2011_ACSM_position_stand]. See [[sci:sci-flexibility]].

drills.name: Wall calf stretch (straight and bent knee)
equipment: wall, rack upright or treadmill rail
drills.summary: Two [[term:static-stretching|static stretches]] for the calf: straight knee for gastrocnemius, bent knee for soleus. Ankle range matters for squat depth and running, both part of your programme.
drills.dose: Full-body B and cardio cool-downs: 2 × 30 s per leg, one straight-knee and one bent-knee hold, left first.
setup: Hands on a wall, left foot back with the toes pointing straight ahead and the heel down.
Front knee bent, weight leaning towards the wall.
execution: Straight-knee hold: back knee straight, heel down, lean the hips forward until the upper calf reaches about 7/10; hold 30 s.
Bent-knee hold: step the back foot in a little and bend that knee, heel still down, until the lower calf stretches; hold 30 s.
Repeat on the right.
cues: Knee over toes in the bent version

errors.error: Heel lifting
errors.fix: Shorten the stance until the heel stays down.

errors.error: Foot turned out with the arch collapsing
errors.fix: Point the toes forward; you should feel the calf, not the inner foot.

drills.progression: Hold longer at a strong 6-7/10, or drop the heel off a step edge.
drills.regression: Shorter stance and a gentler lean.

alternatives.why: Full-range loaded calf work improved flexibility as much as long stretching.
Dynamic ankle range for warm-ups.

drills.whyChosen: Squatting and running both need ankle dorsiflexion, so this is a cheap hedge (inference). Use [[ex:test-knee-wall]] to see whether your ankles need it; our evidence review makes the calves a priority only if that test is limited.
drills.safety: Achilles or heel pain, rather than a muscle stretch, means ease off and follow [[rule:pain]].
drills.mechanism: Gastrocnemius crosses the knee and soleus does not, so bending the knee slackens gastrocnemius and shifts the stretch to soleus (anatomy). Twelve weeks of calf stretching lowered muscle stiffness and lengthened gastrocnemius fascicles by 0.4 cm [@Andrade2020_muscle_nerve_stretching].
drills.evidence: In a 4-week [[term:rct|RCT]], 3 × 60 s of calf stretching at 6-7/10 raised dorsiflexion range by 40% and cut stiffness by 57%, versus 15% and 24% at low intensity [@Nakamura2021_HI_vs_LI_SS]. Muscle-directed stretching added 7.3° of dorsiflexion (95% CI 4.1-10.5) [@Andrade2020_muscle_nerve_stretching]. In one 6-week trial, calf strength training improved flexibility as much as an hour of daily stretching [@Warneke2023_stretch_vs_RT_calf]. Stretching did not prevent injury [@Lauersen2014_injury_prevention]. The knee-to-wall test's minimal detectable change is about 1.6-1.9 cm [@Powden2015_WBLT_reliability].

drills.name: Standing quadriceps stretch
equipment: rack upright or wall to hold
towel if you cannot reach the ankle
drills.summary: A short standing [[term:static-stretching|static stretch]] for the front of the thigh after lower-body and cardio sessions. The pelvic tuck is what makes it reach rectus femoris, the quadriceps head that also crosses the hip.
drills.dose: Lower and cardio cool-downs: 1 × 30 s per side, left leg first.
setup: Stand beside a rack upright and hold it with one hand.
Bend the left knee and hold the left ankle (or a towel looped round it) behind you.
execution: Bring the knees together and tuck the pelvis under until the front of the left thigh stretches at about 6-7/10.
Hold 30 s standing tall; switch sides, holding the support while you stand on your left leg.

errors.error: Arching the lower back with the knee drifting forward
errors.fix: Tuck the pelvis and keep the knees level; the stretch returns to the thigh.

errors.error: Yanking the heel hard into the buttock
errors.fix: Ease off; heavy pressure on the knee is not the aim.

drills.progression: Take the knee slightly behind the hip while keeping the tuck, or use the back-foot-raised version of [[ex:st-hip-flexor]].
drills.regression: Lie on your side and hold the top ankle, or use the towel.

alternatives.why: Kneeling version that also reaches iliopsoas.
Dynamic front-back hip range for warm-ups.

drills.whyChosen: Brief and needs no floor space, so it fits after a run or a lower session (practical convention). Holding a support makes it a safe one-leg stance on your weaker left side.
drills.safety: Stop for pain in the knee itself (as opposed to a thigh stretch) and use the towel or side-lying version.
drills.mechanism: Rectus femoris crosses hip and knee, so it lengthens with knee flexion plus hip extension; the pelvic tuck supplies the hip extension (anatomy).
drills.evidence: In a small [[term:rct|RCT]] (16 untrained young men), static stretching between sets of flywheel squats increased knee-flexion range and isometric knee-extension strength, but quadriceps growth was similar (7.3% vs 8.0%) [@Nakamura2021_interset_SS]. Static stretching in general increases [[term:rom|ROM]] [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM] and does not meaningfully reduce soreness [@Herbert2011_Cochrane_stretch_DOMS].

drills.name: Figure-4 glute stretch
equipment: mat, or a bench for the seated version
drills.summary: A [[term:static-stretching|static stretch]] for the back and side of the hip, made by crossing one ankle over the opposite knee. Do it lying down, or seated on a bench when the floor is busy.
drills.dose: Lower cool-down: 1 × 30 s per side, left first.
setup: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
Cross the left ankle over the right knee and let the left knee fall outwards; flex the left foot (toes towards the shin).
execution: Thread your hands behind the right thigh and draw it towards your chest until the left buttock stretches at about 6-7/10.
Hold 30 s with the head and lower back resting on the mat; switch sides.
cues: Pull the bottom thigh, not the top knee

errors.error: Pain in the crossed knee
errors.fix: Keep the top foot flexed, pull less, or rest the ankle further down the thigh.

errors.error: Tailbone curling off the mat
errors.fix: Pull less; the stretch should stay in the buttock.

drills.progression: Seated on a bench with the ankle over the knee, hinge forward with a long spine; or hold 45-60 s.
drills.regression: Leave the bottom foot on the floor and gently press the top knee away.

alternatives.why: Dynamic hip rotation for warm-ups.
Covers the inner hip if the figure-4 bothers the knee.

drills.whyChosen: It covers hip rotation that squats, lunges and running use but the hamstring stretches miss (practical convention), and the lying version needs no balance or partner.
drills.safety: Stop for knee pain, or for pain running down the back of the leg, which can mean the sciatic nerve near piriformis is irritated (inference).
drills.mechanism: Hip flexion plus external rotation lengthens gluteus maximus and the deep rotators behind the hip joint (anatomy). As with other stretches, early gains are mostly [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]] [@Freitas2018_chronic_stretch_mechanics].
drills.evidence: No glute-specific trial is in our catalogues, so the general evidence applies: chronic static stretching improves [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM] but post-exercise stretching did not speed recovery (very low certainty) and stretching did not prevent injury [@Afonso2021_postexercise_stretch_recovery; @Lauersen2014_injury_prevention]. See [[sci:sci-flexibility]].

drills.name: Adductor rock-back stretch
drills.system: Flexibility: static or slow dynamic stretching
equipment: mat
drills.summary: An inner-thigh stretch from hands and knees: one leg straight out to the side, hips rocking back. It is not in the standard cool-downs; use it as an optional extra or a swap.
drills.dose: Optional: 1-2 × 30 s per side, left first, at about 6-7/10. In a warm-up, use 8-10 slow rocks per side instead of a hold.
setup: Kneel on all fours on a mat.
Straighten the left leg out to the side, foot flat, toes forward, knee in line with the hip.
execution: Keeping the back long, push the hips back towards the right heel until the inner left thigh stretches.
Hold 30 s (or rock in and out slowly); switch sides.

errors.error: Lower back rounding as the hips go back
errors.fix: Stop the rock where the spine starts to round.

errors.error: Toes of the straight leg pointing up, knee twisting
errors.fix: Keep the foot flat and toes forward, or bend that knee slightly.

drills.progression: Move the straight leg further out or slightly forward, or hold longer.
drills.regression: Bend the extended knee to shorten the lever.

alternatives.why: Side-to-side swings as a dynamic version for warm-ups.
A deep loaded squat takes the adductors through a long range (inference).

drills.whyChosen: Useful if the groin feels tight in deep squats or, later, in lateral bounds and agility drills. Rocking is a [[term:dynamic-stretching|dynamic stretching]] option, and static holds under 30 s cost only about 1.1% of performance [@Kay2012_acute_static_stretch], so neither form should blunt the lifting that follows (inference).
drills.safety: Sharp pain high in the groin, rather than a stretch along the thigh, means stop.
drills.mechanism: The adductors run from the pubis to the inner femur; abducting the hip while the hips move back lengthens them, and the straight knee adds gracilis, which crosses the knee (anatomy).
drills.evidence: No adductor-specific trial is in our catalogues. Chronic stretching improves [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] by an effect size of about 1.0 [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM], and resistance training does so too [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM].

drills.name: Doorway chest stretch
equipment: door frame, rack upright or cable-machine frame
drills.summary: A [[term:static-stretching|static stretch]] for the chest and the front of the shoulder. In the gym, a power-rack upright or the side of a cable machine serves as the doorway.
drills.dose: Full-body B and upper cool-downs: 2 × 30 s per side, left first.
setup: Stand side-on to a rack upright with the left forearm vertical against it, elbow at or just below shoulder height.
Stagger the feet, left foot forward.
execution: Step through and turn the chest gently away from the arm until the front of the left chest and shoulder stretch at about 6-7/10.
Hold 30 s with the shoulder blade drawn slightly back and down; switch sides.
cues: Elbow at shoulder height or lower
Turn the chest, not the neck

errors.error: Front of the shoulder poking forward
errors.fix: Draw the shoulder blade back and step through less; the stretch belongs across the chest.

errors.error: Elbow well above shoulder height
errors.fix: Lower it; high positions strain the front of the shoulder (practical convention).

drills.progression: Vary elbow height slightly to bias the upper or lower chest, or hold 45-60 s.
drills.regression: Place the hand rather than the forearm on the frame and take a smaller step.

alternatives.why: Loads the chest through a long range; lifting improves ROM too.
Dynamic shoulder range for upper-body warm-ups.

drills.whyChosen: Pressing work and long desk hours keep the chest working short or sitting short, so maintaining shoulder range is a reasonable aim (inference). A rack upright saves hunting for a doorway.
drills.safety: Tingling or numbness in the arm or hand means nerves rather than muscle are being loaded: lower the elbow and step through less. Skip it if a shoulder has ever dislocated (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: With the forearm fixed, turning the body away moves the arm backwards relative to the trunk (horizontal abduction), lengthening pectoralis major and the anterior deltoid (anatomy).
drills.evidence: No chest-specific trial is in our catalogues. Static stretching improves [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM]; resistance training does so about as well, more in untrained people (ES 1.04) [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM]. At practical doses stretching adds trivial muscle growth at most ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.12, unclear) [@Arntz2024_SS_hypertrophy_meta], so it is not a hypertrophy tool.

drills.name: Kneeling lat stretch (bench)
equipment: flat bench
mat or towel for the knees
optional light dowel
drills.summary: A [[term:static-stretching|static stretch]] for the lats and the long head of the triceps, kneeling with the elbows on a bench. It protects the overhead range that pull-ups, pulldowns and shoulder presses use.
drills.dose: Full-body A and upper cool-downs: 2 × 30 s.
setup: Kneel facing a flat bench, knees hip-width and slightly behind the hips.
Rest both elbows on the bench edge, shoulder-width, palms together or holding a dowel; bend the elbows so the hands drop behind the head.
execution: Sit the hips back and let the chest sink towards the floor until the sides of the back and the backs of the arms stretch at about 6-7/10.
Hold 30 s, breathing into the ribs; come up, rest briefly, repeat.

errors.error: Arching the lower back so the chest drops without any lat stretch
errors.fix: Tuck the pelvis slightly, keep the ribs down and sink less.

errors.error: Elbows sliding wide
errors.fix: Keep them shoulder-width, or hold a dowel to fix the spacing.

drills.progression: Hold 45-60 s, or work one side at a time with a side reach in child's pose, left side first.
drills.regression: Child's pose with the arms forward on the floor, or straighten the elbows to take the triceps out.

alternatives.why: Loads the lats from a full stretch at the top; lifting improves ROM too.
Dynamic overhead range before upper sessions.

drills.whyChosen: Overhead pressing and full-range pulling need shoulder flexion, which tight lats often limit in beginners (practical convention). The bench lets gravity do the work without a partner.
drills.safety: Pinching at the front or top of the shoulder means you have gone past a useful range; back off. Pad the knees.
drills.mechanism: The lats run from the pelvis and lower spine to the front of the upper humerus, so arms overhead with the trunk fixed lengthens them; bending the elbows adds the triceps long head, which crosses the shoulder (anatomy). Early gains are mostly [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]] [@Weppler2010_sensory_theory].
drills.evidence: No lat-specific trial is in our catalogues. Static stretching improves [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] by an effect size of about 1.0 [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM], and passive stretching, as here, more than active [@Arntz2023_chronic_SS_strength]. See [[sci:sci-flexibility]].

drills.name: Overhead triceps stretch
equipment: none
drills.summary: An optional standing [[term:static-stretching|static stretch]] for the back of the upper arm. The kneeling lat stretch already covers this muscle, so use it as a quick swap rather than an extra.
drills.dose: Optional: 1 × 30 s per side, left first, at about 6/10.
setup: Stand tall and raise the left arm overhead.
Bend the left elbow so the hand drops behind the head towards the upper back.
execution: With the right hand, ease the left elbow back and slightly towards the head until the back of the upper arm stretches.
Hold 30 s; switch sides.

errors.error: Arching the lower back to get the elbow further back
errors.fix: Brace lightly, keep the ribs down and accept a smaller range.

errors.error: Pushing the head forward under the arm
errors.fix: Keep the head level and the neck long.

drills.progression: Hold a towel behind the back with the lower hand and walk the hands closer.
drills.regression: Rest the elbow against a door frame or rack upright instead of pulling.

alternatives.why: Covers the triceps long head and the lats in one position.
Trains the long head through its stretched range under load.

drills.whyChosen: Kept as an option because it takes a minute and needs no equipment; nothing in your profile makes it a priority (practical convention).
drills.safety: Shoulder pinching or tingling down the arm means stop and use the lat-stretch version.
drills.mechanism: The long head of the triceps crosses both shoulder and elbow, so full shoulder flexion plus full elbow flexion lengthens it (anatomy).
drills.evidence: No triceps-specific trial is in our catalogues. Static stretching improves [[term:rom|range of motion (ROM)]] [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM], but self-selected, low-intensity passive stretching did not change muscle structure in human studies [@Nunes2020_stretch_hypertrophy_review], so do not count it towards arm growth.

drills.name: Easy cool-down (walk or cycle)
equipment: treadmill or stationary bike, or walk outdoors
drills.summary: A few minutes of very easy walking or cycling between the last hard work and your stretches. It is for comfort and a calm transition; it will not speed recovery or prevent [[term:doms|delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)]].
drills.dose: Lifting cool-downs: 2 min easy walk or cycle. Cardio cool-down: 3 min easy. Effort about 2/10 on the [[term:rpe|RPE]] scale; up to 5 min after intervals if you prefer.
setup: Treadmill at a slow walk with no incline, or a bike at very light resistance.
Have water and your stretching spot ready.
execution: Move at an effort where you could chat easily while breathing and heart rate come down.
Go to your stretches once breathing feels normal.

errors.error: Turning it into extra moderate cardio
errors.fix: Keep it at about 2/10; extra aerobic work belongs in the main session.

errors.error: Stopping abruptly and lying down right after hard intervals
errors.fix: Walk for 3-5 min first; light movement helps blood return from the legs (practical convention).

drills.progression: None needed; it stays short and easy.
drills.regression: Walk around the gym floor if the machines are taken.

alternatives.why: Same machines and effort, used at the start of a session.
If you want more aerobic volume, extend into a steady session instead.

drills.whyChosen: A brief, low-cost transition that many people find more comfortable after hard work. Because the evidence for recovery benefits is weak, it is kept to 2-3 min and is optional (see [[dec:D10]]).
drills.safety: Light-headedness after intervals means keep walking slowly rather than sitting. Chest pain, unusual breathlessness or palpitations mean stop and get help (see [[plan:safety]]).
drills.mechanism: Light activity speeds blood lactate clearance and may help cardiorespiratory recovery [@VanHooren2018_cooldown]. Soreness, however, appears to come from sensitised muscle pain receptors (shown mainly in rat studies) [@Mizumura2024_DOMS_neurochemistry], so clearing lactate faster does not mean less soreness.
drills.evidence: A review found active cool-downs largely ineffective for same-day and next-day performance, injury prevention and soreness, and noted they can impair glycogen resynthesis [@VanHooren2018_cooldown]. In an [[term:rct|RCT]], a 10-min cool-down had no effect on soreness at 48 h (0 mm on a 100-mm scale, 95% CI -11 to 11) [@Law2007_warmup_cooldown_DOMS]. See [[sci:sci-recovery]].
