drills.name: Steady aerobic session (moderate, conversational)
equipment: treadmill with incline (default)
or stationary bike, elliptical, rower, or a brisk outdoor walk
drills.summary: Continuous [[term:mict|moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT)]] at a pace where you can still speak in full sentences. It is the base of your aerobic work: it builds [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]], adds to weekly energy expenditure and teaches you to judge effort without a heart-rate monitor.
drills.dose: [[phase:p0]]: 20 min at [[term:rpe|RPE]] 3-4/10. [[phase:p1]] and maintenance ([[phase:pm]]): the phase's set minutes at RPE 3-4, progressed by duration on the same machine ([[rule:cardio-progression]]). [[phase:p2]]: 10 min brisk walking or easy cycling after the run-walk.
setup: Default: treadmill walk at about 4.5-6 km/h and 5-12% incline, adjusted to the effort target (practical convention).
Note the machine, speed and incline (or bike level) so you can repeat them.
execution: Build up over 3-5 min, then set speed or incline so breathing is deeper but full sentences are still possible (the [[term:talk-test|talk test]]): RPE 3-4.
Hold that effort for the set time; if you are down to short phrases, slow down.
Log duration, settings and session RPE in Hevy.

errors.error: Drifting into a hard effort with only short phrases possible
errors.fix: Ease off; moderately hard steady work is neither easy enough to accumulate nor hard enough to count as intervals.

errors.error: Holding the handrails on a steep incline
errors.fix: Lower the incline until you can walk hands-free; holding on reduces the work.

drills.progression: Add time first (about 5 min at a time) at RPE 3-4; as you get fitter, the same RPE will need more speed or incline.
drills.regression: Shorter sessions, flat walking, or the bike if shins or knees complain.
drills.away: Walk briskly outdoors, or indoors on stairs or long corridors, at the same [[term:rpe|RPE]] 3–4 (full sentences); hills or stairs make it harder at walking speed, and a hike, swim, bike ride, dance or martial-arts class of similar length also counts. Without a treadmill's incline, a flat walk may drop below RPE 3 as you get fitter: walk faster, choose a hilly route or carry a backpack with a few kilograms of water bottles (practical convention). Progress by time, as in the gym (in [[phase:pa|Away mode]] the session is 30 min in week 1 and 35 min after that), and run only if your phase already includes running ([[rule:running]]). In Indian midday heat, walk in shade or on an indoor stairwell and carry water (practical convention).

alternatives.why: Longer weekend version, including hikes and classes.
Introduces running from Phase 2.

drills.whyChosen: Incline walking is low-impact and easy to control, and avoids novice running injury risk while fitness builds (inference). The talk test needs no equipment, which suits training alone without a monitor ([[dec:D11]], [[tool:intensity]]). Done after lifting, it protects lifting quality: resistance-first order gave larger lower-body strength gains [@Eddens2018_sequenceMA].
drills.safety: At 13:00, about an hour after waking, build up gently over the first 5 min. Stop for chest pain, faintness or unusual breathlessness ([[plan:safety]]). For outdoor walks in Indian midday heat, choose shade and carry water (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: In 16 untrained men, early VO₂max gains depended mainly on blood and heart: more plasma and red-cell volume and a higher maximal cardiac output, the product of heart rate and [[term:stroke-volume|stroke volume]] [@Montero2015_haematologicalVO2peak]. Muscle mitochondrial content rose similarly with continuous, interval and sprint training once dose was accounted for [@Molmen2024_mitoCapillaryMetaRegression].
drills.evidence: Continuous training raised VO₂max by about 4.9 mL/kg/min versus controls [@Milanovic2015_HITvsCET_VO2maxMA]; in one trial, untrained men running 3 × 60 min/week gained 21.5% in relative VO₂max in 12 weeks, partly through weight loss [@Milanovic2015_untrainedMenRunningRCT]. Comfortable speech marked intensities up to about the first [[term:ventilatory-threshold|ventilatory threshold]], mostly in cardiac patients [@Vieira2022_talkTestSR]; fixed heart-rate zones misplace individual thresholds [@Meixner2025_zone2MarkerVariability], and [[term:zone-2|zone 2]] is not uniquely effective [@Storoschuk2025_zone2Review]. In trials in adults with overweight or obesity, each 30 min/week of aerobic exercise was linked to 0.52 kg lower body weight [@Jayedi2024_aerobicWeightLossDoseResponse].

drills.name: Run-walk session
drills.system: Aerobic: easy running with walk breaks

primary: running tolerance of tendons, bones and calves

equipment: running shoes you find comfortable
treadmill, track or flat shaded route
interval timer
drills.summary: Alternating easy running and brisk walking so your legs adapt to running gradually. For a novice, running probably carries the highest injury rate of anything in your programme (inference), so the walk breaks and the progression rules matter more than pace.
drills.dose: [[phase:p2]]: the week's run-walk pattern from the progression table ([[tool:running]]), running at [[term:rpe|RPE]] 4-5 (short sentences still possible) and walking briskly between, then 10 min brisk walking or easy cycling.
setup: Warm up with 5 min brisk walking.
Set the interval timer to the week's run and walk times.
execution: Run easily: short, quick, quiet steps, upright posture, relaxed arms.
Walk briskly in the walk intervals; do not stop.
Afterwards note any pain (0-10) and its location, and log time run, total time and RPE.

errors.error: Running too fast because the run intervals feel short
errors.fix: Slow to a pace where you could speak in short sentences; walk breaks are not recovery from a sprint.

errors.error: A big jump in running time on a good day
errors.fix: Obey the spike rule: no single session more than 10% longer than your longest run in the past 30 days.

drills.progression: Follow the table, moving on only after a week in which any pain stayed at 3/10 or below and settled by the next morning. Pain that lasts into the next day or changes your stride means hold or step back a week ([[rule:running]]).
drills.regression: Repeat the previous week's pattern, or switch that session to incline walking or the bike.
drills.away: It needs only shoes and a timer, so keep your phase's run-walk pattern and the spike rule while away ([[rule:running]]); in [[phase:pa|Away mode]] it can replace the steady session. Choose a flat, even route, and on unfamiliar roads or surfaces run the first session a little easier than usual (inference). If your phase has not reached running yet, walk briskly instead ([[ex:cardio-steady]]). In Indian midday heat, pick shade and carry water (practical convention), and stop for pain that changes your stride ([[term:pain-monitoring|pain-monitoring model]]).

alternatives.why: Incline walking or bike when the legs need a break from impact.
The running test this work prepares you for.

drills.whyChosen: Per hour of running, novices were injured about twice as often as recreational runners (17.8 vs 7.7 per 1000 h) [@Videbaek2015_runningInjuryIncidence], and no previous running experience is a risk factor [@vanPoppel2021_riskfactors], so exposure grows in small steps ([[dec:D14]]). In a cohort of mostly experienced runners, single runs more than 10% longer than the longest in the past 30 days were associated with a higher injury hazard (HRR 1.64 for 10-30% longer; observational) [@Frandsen2025_spikes].
drills.safety: Use the [[term:pain-monitoring|pain-monitoring model]]: mild pain (up to 3/10) that settles by the next morning is acceptable; sharp, worsening pain or limping is not. At 13:00 in Indian heat, use a treadmill or shaded route and carry water (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: Tendon and bone adapt more slowly than heart and lungs, so fitness can outrun tissue tolerance; walk breaks cap the impact per session (inference). In a laboratory study, a step rate 5-10% above your natural one reduced energy absorbed at the knee [@Heiderscheit2011_steprate].
drills.evidence: A graded '10% per week' programme did not reduce injuries versus a standard one (20.8% vs 20.3%) [@Buist2008_GRONORUN], though few runners followed either schedule exactly [@Nielsen2020_compliance]. Higher step rate immediately lowered knee flexion and patellofemoral stress (biomechanical measures, not injuries) [@Anderson2022_steprate]. Harder shoes raised injury risk in lighter runners [@Malisoux2020_cushioning], pronated feet did not [@Nielsen2014_pronation], and shoes perceived as comfortable and cushioned were linked to lower risk [@Malisoux2025_comfortperception]. See [[sci:sci-athletic]].

drills.name: Introductory intervals (1 min hard / 2 min easy)
equipment: stationary bike (preferred) or rower
interval timer
drills.summary: Your first exposure to [[term:hiit|high-intensity interval training (HIIT)]]: 1-min efforts with generous easy recovery. The aim is to learn what hard but controlled feels like, finishing every repetition at the same output, before moving to 4 × 4.
drills.dose: [[phase:p1]]: the phase's set number (typically 6-8) of 1:00 hard ([[term:rpe|RPE]] 7-8) / 2:00 easy (RPE 2-3), after an 8-10 min warm-up building from easy to moderate; finish with [[ex:cd-easy]].
setup: Bike or rower; set the interval timer.
Warm up 8-10 min, the last 2 min at a moderate effort.
execution: Hard minute: raise resistance or cadence to RPE 7-8 (breathing hard, a few words possible); note the watts or pace shown.
Easy 2 min: pedal or row very lightly (RPE 2-3) while breathing settles.
Aim to match the first repetition's output on the last; log each repetition's RPE and output in Hevy.

errors.error: Going all-out early and fading
errors.fix: Start at the low end of RPE 7; raise it only in the last two repetitions.

errors.error: Working too hard in the recoveries
errors.fix: Keep the easy minutes easy so each hard minute is high quality.

drills.progression: Build to 8 repetitions, then move to [[ex:cardio-int-4x4]] in Phase 2 ([[rule:cardio-progression]]).
drills.regression: Fewer repetitions (4-5) or RPE 6-7 if you finish wrecked, sleep poorly, or your next lower-body session suffers.

alternatives.why: Moderate continuous work if you are unwell or under-recovered.
The longer-interval format this session prepares you for.

drills.whyChosen: Bike or rower avoids impact and the injuries seen with all-out treadmill sprints [@Helgerud2023_HIITvsSIT_femaleRCT]. Even very short, low-volume HIIT improved VO₂max versus controls ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.79-1.65), and longer intervals did better [@Wen2019_HIITprotocolsMA]; the 1-min/2-min format is a learning step (practical convention). See [[dec:D11]].
drills.safety: At 13:00 you are early in your biological day, and performance appears to track internal rather than clock time [@FacerChilds2018_chronotype]; warm-ups reduced such time-of-day differences [@Kusumoto2021_diurnal_variation], so never cut the warm-up. Training alone, stop for chest pain, faintness, palpitations or unusual breathlessness ([[plan:safety]]). Keep it off your heaviest leg day.
drills.mechanism: Hard efforts drive the heart near its maximal output; HIIT increased plasma volume, maximal [[term:stroke-volume|stroke volume]] (+14.1%) and cardiac output (+12.6%) [@Rosenblat2022_centralPeripheralMA]. Exercise-induced [[term:pgc1a|PGC-1α]] signalling for [[term:mitochondrial-biogenesis|mitochondrial biogenesis]] rises with intensity [@Granata2018_PGC1aPrescription].
drills.evidence: HIIT raised [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] by 5.98 mL/kg/min versus no exercise (moderate certainty) and by 1.39 more than continuous training (low certainty) [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT]. Adding HIIT to resistance training did not change hypertrophy, with slightly smaller lower-body strength gains (ES -0.25) [@Sabag2018_HIITconcurrentMA]. See [[sci:sci-aerobic]] and [[sci:sci-concurrent]].

drills.name: 4 x 4-minute intervals

secondary: leg muscles (bike, uphill walk or run) or whole body (rower)

equipment: stationary bike, rower, or treadmill with incline
interval timer
optional chest-strap heart-rate monitor
drills.summary: Your main [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] session: four 4-min hard bouts with 3 min of active recovery, a format with a strong trial record among [[term:hiit|high-intensity interval training (HIIT)]] protocols. Hard means only a few words possible by the end of each bout, not all-out.
drills.dose: [[phase:p2]]: the phase's set number of hard bouts ([[term:rpe|RPE]] 8-9) with 3:00 easy (RPE 3) between, building to 4 × 4 min; in weeks 1-3 the hard bouts last 3 min, to learn pacing. [[phase:p3]] and [[phase:pm]]: as set in the phase plan. Warm up 8-10 min and finish with [[ex:cd-easy]]; about 35-40 min in all.
setup: Pick one machine for the block and set the timer to 4:00 hard / 3:00 easy.
Warm up 8-10 min, building from easy to moderate, with two or three 20-30 s pick-ups.
execution: Each bout: settle over the first minute at a pace you expect to hold; by the end you should reach RPE 8-9, a few words only.
Recoveries: 3 min of easy pedalling, rowing or walking at RPE 3, not standing still.
Pace evenly so bout 4 matches bout 1; log each bout's output and RPE in Hevy.

errors.error: Starting the first bout too fast and fading
errors.fix: Begin each bout slightly below target; the effort climbs on its own as the minutes pass.

errors.error: Uphill walking that no longer gets hard enough as you get fitter
errors.fix: Add speed, switch to an uphill jog, or move to the bike or rower.

drills.progression: Hold 4 × 4 at the same RPE while output (watts, speed or incline) rises. Add a second weekly session only when the phase plan calls for it and lifting progress and sleep are unaffected; rotate the machine every 4-6 weeks ([[rule:cardio-progression]]).
drills.regression: 3 × 4 min, 4 × 3 min, or RPE 7-8; after illness, restart with [[ex:cardio-int-intro]] ([[rule:illness]]).
drills.away: Without a bike, rower or treadmill, do [[ex:cardio-noeq-intervals]] instead: 2-min hard climbs of a stairwell or a hill at the same RPE 8–9, walking down easily between. If running is already part of your phase, hard running efforts can replace the climbs, within the spike rule ([[rule:running]]). A bodyweight circuit is the last resort, because in pooled trials bodyweight-only intervals improved cardiorespiratory fitness less than running or cycling training, intervals or continuous ([[term:smd|SMD]] −0.40) [@Scoubeau2022_wholeBodyHIITmeta]. On stairs, hold the rail and never hurry down.

alternatives.why: Shorter efforts when returning from a break.
Phase 3 option for variety; smaller VO₂max gains in trials.

drills.whyChosen: In an 8-week trial in moderately trained men, 4 × 4 raised VO₂max by 7.2%, more than work-matched continuous or threshold running [@Helgerud2007_4x4RCT], and in well-trained men it beat sprint intervals (+6.5% vs +3.3%) [@Hov2022_HIITvsSIT_RCT]. Intervals of 2 min or longer with at least 15 min of hard work were the configurations that outperformed continuous training [@Wen2019_HIITprotocolsMA]. See [[dec:D13]].
drills.safety: The hardest regular session you will do alone: keep your phone near, train when staff are around, and stop for chest pain, faintness or palpitations ([[plan:safety]]). Schedule it after upper-body lifting or on a non-lifting day, at least a day before your heaviest lower session (inference).
drills.mechanism: Minutes near VO₂max in each bout load the heart's pumping capacity; [[term:stroke-volume|stroke volume]] rose about 10% after interval training [@Helgerud2007_4x4RCT]. By the [[term:fick-principle|Fick principle]], VO₂max is cardiac output times arterial-venous O₂ difference, and in a small study gains after the first weeks came mostly from cardiac output [@Murias2010_timeCourse].
drills.evidence: Trials targeted 90-95% of [[term:hrmax|HRmax]]; a chest strap will read lower early in each bout because heart rate lags effort (standard physiology). Equations put your HRmax near 186 bpm [@Tanaka2001_HRmax], but about 95% of individuals lie within roughly ±21 bpm of any equation's value [@Nes2013_HUNT_HRmax], so trust RPE over a watch. The edge over continuous training is small (1.39 mL/kg/min, low certainty) [@Strauss2026_CochraneHIIT]. Non-response fell with dose and vanished at higher weekly frequencies [@MonteroLundby2017_nonresponse]. See [[sci:sci-aerobic]].

drills.name: Sprint intervals (bike)
drills.system: Anaerobic and aerobic: sprint interval training
equipment: stationary bike with adjustable resistance (air bike or spin bike)
interval timer
drills.summary: An optional Phase 3 session of [[term:sit|sprint interval training (SIT)]]: a handful of 20-30 s near all-out efforts on a bike with long easy recoveries. It is time-efficient and adds variety, but it does not replace 4 × 4 for [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]].
drills.dose: [[phase:p3]], optional: 4-6 × 20-30 s near all-out with 2-4 min very easy pedalling between, after a 10-min warm-up with 2-3 short build-ups. Only after months of regular interval training.
setup: Saddle at hip height, feet secured; check the resistance control before you start.
Warm up 10 min, including two or three 10-s accelerations to about 80% effort.
execution: Sprint: raise the resistance and pedal as hard as you can sustain for 20-30 s, seated or in a controlled standing position.
Recover 2-4 min at very light resistance, legs still turning.
Log peak or average watts per sprint; end the session if output falls more than about 20% (practical convention).

errors.error: Resistance so low that the legs spin out of control
errors.fix: Add resistance until cadence stays controlled at maximal effort.

errors.error: Doing the sprints on a treadmill
errors.fix: Use the bike: all-out treadmill sprinting caused 8 injuries in one trial.

drills.progression: Add one sprint (up to 6) or 5 s per sprint across weeks; no more than one sprint session a week (inference).
drills.regression: 4 × 20 s at about 85-90% effort, or return to [[ex:cardio-int-4x4]].

alternatives.why: Larger VO₂max gains in head-to-head trials.
Power training without the metabolic strain.

drills.whyChosen: Sprints matched continuous training for aerobic capacity in far less time (d 0.04 versus continuous) [@Gist2014_SITmeta] and were, per hour, the most time-efficient stimulus for mitochondrial content [@Molmen2024_mitoCapillaryMetaRegression]. It stays optional because 4 × 4 raised VO₂max more in head-to-head trials [@Hov2022_HIITvsSIT_RCT], and the bike avoids the strains seen with treadmill sprints [@Helgerud2023_HIITvsSIT_femaleRCT]. See [[dec:D16]].
drills.safety: The most strenuous session in the programme: do it only when healthy and rested, when staff or other members are around, and stop for chest pain, faintness or nausea that does not settle ([[plan:safety]]). Keep it apart from heavy leg days.
drills.mechanism: The first seconds of an all-out effort lean on the [[term:phosphocreatine|phosphocreatine system]] and glycolysis (standard physiology). Repeated sprints still drive aerobic adaptations: citrate synthase activity rose 15.7% after SIT [@Rosenblat2022_centralPeripheralMA].
drills.evidence: SIT improved aerobic capacity by about 3.6 mL/kg/min (about 8%) [@Gist2014_SITmeta], but studies comparing it with continuous training had unclear risk of bias [@Bonafiglia2021_SITvsMICTbias]. In well-trained women, only 4 × 4, not sprints, increased VO₂max (+7.3%) [@Helgerud2023_HIITvsSIT_femaleRCT]. In concurrent training, sprint formats did not impair jump gains, whereas short and long HIIT formats did (subgroup analysis of few trials) [@Kikuchi2026_HIITconcurrentMA].

drills.name: Tempo session
equipment: treadmill, bike, rower or a flat outdoor route
timer
drills.summary: A Phase 3 session of 15-25 min held at a 'comfortably hard' effort, around your [[term:lactate-threshold|lactate threshold]]. It trains the pace you can sustain and is useful before a running test, but it supplements 4 × 4 intervals rather than replacing them.
drills.dose: [[phase:p3]]: 15-25 min continuous at [[term:rpe|RPE]] 5-6 (short phrases only) after a 10-min warm-up; finish with [[ex:cd-easy]]. At most one a week, in place of an easy session (inference).
setup: Warm up 10 min, building from easy to moderate.
If a test is coming, use the machine or route you will test on (e.g. the treadmill before [[ex:test-run-2400]]).
execution: Settle into an effort where you can speak only in short phrases (RPE 5-6) and hold it steady.
If it climbs above RPE 6 in the first half, slow slightly; the last 5 min should feel hard but controlled.
Log distance or average output, duration and RPE.

errors.error: Turning it into a race
errors.fix: Hold RPE 5-6; if you could not continue another 10 min at that pace, it is too hard.

errors.error: Adding tempo work on top of everything else
errors.fix: Swap it for an easy session; a week full of moderately hard sessions adds fatigue without extra VO₂max gain.

drills.progression: Extend from 15 to 25 min at the same RPE, then let pace or output rise.
drills.regression: 2 × 10 min with 2 min easy between, or return to [[ex:cardio-steady]].

alternatives.why: The stronger VO₂max stimulus.
Easier aerobic volume when recovery is limited.

drills.whyChosen: Phase 3 adds variety and test-specific pacing ([[dec:D16]]). In recreational athletes, pyramidal intensity distributions, which include some threshold work, tended to raise VO₂max more than polarised ones [@Rosenblat2025_TID_IPDnetworkMA], so a small dose is reasonable (inference).
drills.safety: As with every hard session done alone, stop for chest pain, faintness or palpitations ([[plan:safety]]). Outdoors at 13:00 in Indian heat, effort rises quickly at the same pace: use the treadmill or bike on hot days (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: Being limited to short phrases puts you beyond the point where speech first becomes difficult, which lies near the [[term:ventilatory-threshold|ventilatory threshold]] [@Persinger2004_talkTest]; the individual anaerobic threshold corresponded to about 13.6 on the 6-20 Borg scale [@Scherr2013_RPE]. Holding effort here trains sustainable pace more than maximal oxygen uptake (inference).
drills.evidence: Lactate-threshold running at 85% of [[term:hrmax|HRmax]] raised VO₂max less than 4 × 4 intervals in an 8-week trial [@Helgerud2007_4x4RCT], and threshold-focused training produced no further gains in well-trained athletes [@Stoggl2014_polarizedRCT]. That is why tempo waits until Phase 3 and stays small. See [[sci:sci-aerobic]].

drills.name: Long easy session (hike, ride, run-walk, dance class)
equipment: depends on the activity: walking or hiking shoes, a bike, or a class
drills.summary: A weekly long session at easy effort, done as something you enjoy: a hike (ideally with climbs), a long ride, a run-walk, or a dance or martial-arts class. It adds aerobic volume cheaply and breaks the gym routine.
drills.dose: [[phase:p3]]: the phase's set minutes (45-90 min) at [[term:rpe|RPE]] 3-4, full sentences possible, or a class of similar length. Usually on a non-lifting day.
setup: Plan the route or class in advance; carry water, and food for anything over about 75 min (practical convention).
If it includes running, apply the spike rule to the running time.
execution: Keep the effort conversational for most of the session; on climbs, slow down so you could still speak in sentences.
Classes set their own intensity; that is fine if most of the time feels moderate.
Log duration, activity and session RPE, and rate enjoyment 1-5.

errors.error: Turning a hike or ride into a race
errors.fix: Hold RPE 3-4; the long session works through time, not intensity.

errors.error: A run-walk far longer than any recent run
errors.fix: Keep running time within 10% of your longest run in the past 30 days ([[rule:running]]).

drills.progression: Add 10-15 min at a time up to 90 min, or pick routes with more climbing.
drills.regression: Shorter or flatter route, or a 45-min class.

alternatives.why: Gym version when time or weather rules out going outside.
For a running-focused long session.

drills.whyChosen: Enjoyment keeps people training, and these options have outcome evidence: dance matched other exercise for cardiovascular fitness and did better for body composition [@FongYan2018_danceMA], and recreational soccer raised VO₂max by 24.2% in untrained men [@Milanovic2015_untrainedMenRunningRCT]. Since you train alone, a class or group hike also adds company. See [[dec:D16]] and [[sci:sci-behaviour]].
drills.safety: Hike with someone or share your route and expected return time. In Indian heat, avoid exposed midday stretches, drink regularly, and stop for dizziness, confusion or cramping (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: Long easy work accumulates training volume, the main driver of mitochondrial content [@Granata2018_mitoContentVsFunction], and adds energy expenditure without the recovery cost of hard sessions (inference).
drills.evidence: Walking groups raised [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] by 2.66 mL/kg/min and lowered body fat by 1.31 percentage points [@Hanson2015_walkinggroups]. Fat loss rose roughly linearly with aerobic minutes up to 300 min/week [@Jayedi2024_aerobicWeightLossDoseResponse], though people tend to eat back part of the energy spent [@Martin2019_EMECHANIC]. WHO advises 150-300 min/week of moderate activity [@Bull2020_WHOguidelines].

drills.name: Pogo hops
equipment: firm, non-slip floor; trainers
drills.summary: Small, quick, continuous two-foot hops driven by the ankles with almost straight knees, spending as little time on the floor as possible. The entry-level [[term:plyometrics|plyometric]] drill: it trains the calf-Achilles spring used in running and jumping.
drills.dose: 2 x 12 contacts in the athletic lower-day warm-up, about 60-90 s between sets; they count towards your plyometric contact total. Full intent on each contact: short ground contact, not maximal height.
setup: Stand tall, feet hip-width, weight on the balls of the feet.
Arms relaxed, or a small rhythmic arm swing.
execution: Hop 5-10 cm off the floor using the ankles; the knees stay nearly straight.
Land on the balls of the feet and rebound at once, as if the floor were hot.
Keep a steady rhythm for 12 contacts; end the set early if contacts become slow or heavy.

errors.error: Bending knees and hips to jump higher.
errors.fix: Keep the legs nearly straight; height is not the goal.

errors.error: Heels crashing down on each landing.
errors.fix: Stay on the balls of the feet and lower the hops.

errors.error: Carrying on when contacts slow down.
errors.fix: End the set; quick contacts are the training stimulus.

drills.progression: Slightly higher hops, then forward-backward or side-to-side pogos, then single-leg pogos (left first) in later weeks.
drills.regression: Lower hops, or calf raises finished with a small bounce.

alternatives.why: A lower-intensity bouncing activity dosed by time.
Builds calf and Achilles strength without impact.

drills.whyChosen: Running loads the calf-Achilles spring with every step, and pogos train it in small, controllable doses before bigger jumps (practical convention). Untrained people gained more lower-limb stiffness from plyometric training (ES 0.46) than trained people [@Moran2023_stiffness]. See [[dec:D17]].
drills.safety: Skip them on days with Achilles, calf or shin pain, and hold progression if soreness lasts more than a day; after hard stretch-shortening exercise, function can dip again around day 2 [@Nicol2006_SSC]. Avoid them the day before your longest run (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: Each hop is a short-contact [[term:ssc|stretch-shortening cycle]]: the calf is pre-activated before landing, stretched under load and recoils at once, with a strong stretch-reflex contribution [@Nicol2006_SSC]. Training improves the [[term:rsi|reactive strength index]] (jump height relative to contact time; ES 0.54) [@RamirezCampillo2023_RSI], and loading stiffens tendons mainly by changing their material properties (modulus) [@Lazarczuk2022_tendon].
drills.evidence: Lower-limb stiffness improved most with fewer than 250 jumps per week (ES 0.50) and not at all above 500 per week [@Moran2023_stiffness]; reactive-strength gains were similar up to about 1080 total jumps as with more [@RamirezCampillo2023_RSI]. Plyometric training also improved balance (ES 0.46) about as much as balance training [@Ramachandran2021_plyobalance]. The 2 x 12 dose is practical convention within those ranges.

drills.name: Box jump (low box, step down)

primary: quadriceps, glutes and calves (hip, knee and ankle extension)

equipment: stable plyo box or step 30-45 cm high; a soft-topped box if available
drills.summary: From standing, you jump onto a low box, land softly in a quarter squat, stand up and step down. The box cuts landing impact compared with jumping on the floor, and stepping down avoids the high-impact landing of jumping off.
drills.dose: 3 x 4 in the athletic lower-day warm-up, box 30-45 cm, a full reset between reps and about 60-90 s between sets; each jump counts as one contact.
setup: Check that the box is stable and cannot slide; place it on a non-slip floor away from walkways.
Stand about 30 cm from the box, feet hip-width.
execution: Swing the arms back and dip into a quick quarter squat.
Jump explosively, swinging the arms forward and up.
Land softly on the whole foot, knees over the toes, at about the depth of the take-off dip.
Stand fully, then step down one foot at a time, alternating the leading foot (left first).
Reset completely before the next jump.

errors.error: A box so high that you land in a deep squat.
errors.fix: Use a lower box; landing depth should match take-off depth.

errors.error: Knees caving in on landing.
errors.fix: Lower box, slower reset, knees over toes.

errors.error: Jumping down off the box.
errors.fix: Always step down; the landing from a jump down is a much larger load.

drills.progression: More take-off intent rather than a higher box; a slightly higher box only once landings stay shallow and quiet (practical convention).
drills.regression: A lower step, or a jump in place with a held landing.

alternatives.why: Horizontal jump if no box is free.
Smaller, ankle-driven jumps on a day when you feel less fresh.

drills.whyChosen: Box jumps train take-off power while limiting landing load, which suits a novice without a coach, and stepping down removes the riskiest part (practical convention). Plyometric training raised countermovement jump height by 8.7% on average [@Markovic2007_vertjump]. See [[dec:D17]].
drills.safety: Missing the box is the main hazard: use a stable box, ideally soft-topped, at a height you clear easily, and check the space around and behind it in a busy gym. Stop with knee or Achilles pain.
drills.mechanism: The countermovement dip loads the hip, knee and ankle extensors just before take-off, so the [[term:ssc|stretch-shortening cycle]] adds to the push [@Nicol2006_SSC]. Gains in jump height probably come mostly from better coordination and faster force production (inference), with small-to-moderate increases in muscle size, largest in the knee extensors (overall SMD 0.47) [@Arntz2022_hypertrophy].
drills.evidence: Plyometric training improved countermovement jump height by 8.7% (95% CI 7.0-10.4%) [@Markovic2007_vertjump]. Larger gains came with programmes longer than 10 weeks and more than 20 sessions, and adding weight gave no extra benefit [@deVillarreal2009_dose]. The low box and step-down rule are practical convention.

drills.name: Standing broad jump
equipment: about 5 m of clear, non-slip floor
drills.summary: From standing, you swing the arms and jump forward as far as you can, landing on both feet and holding the landing. It trains horizontal power, driven mainly by the hips, plus landing control; the same movement is your [[ex:test-broad-jump|broad-jump test]].
drills.dose: 3 x 3 with a full reset between reps and about 60-90 s between sets; each jump counts as one plyometric contact. It is not in a fixed warm-up block: use it as a swap for [[ex:plyo-box-jump]] when no box is free, or within a plyometric block.
setup: Toes behind a line, feet hip-width.
Check that at least 3 m ahead is clear of people and equipment.
execution: Swing the arms back while hinging at the hips and bending the knees.
Drive the arms forward and extend hips, knees and ankles to jump forward and slightly up.
Land on both feet with knees bent and in line with the toes; hold the landing for 2 s.
Walk back and reset fully before the next jump.

errors.error: Landing stiff-legged or falling forward.
errors.fix: Jump a little shorter and absorb with hips and knees; every landing must be held.

errors.error: Knees caving in on landing.
errors.fix: Shorter jumps, landing with the knees over the toes.

errors.error: Rushing the reps.
errors.fix: Full reset: each jump is a separate maximal effort.

drills.progression: More distance; later, two consecutive broad jumps with a held final landing (practical convention).
drills.regression: Shorter, submaximal jumps focused on the landing.

alternatives.why: Vertical jump with a lower landing load.
Explosive hip extension without any landing.

drills.whyChosen: Horizontal jumping depends heavily on hip extension, which ties it to your hinge training, and it needs no equipment. Holding each landing rehearses braking, which change of direction also needs (practical convention). See [[dec:D17]].
drills.safety: Use a non-slip surface and trainers. Stop with knee, hip or lower-back pain. Avoid maximal jumps the day after heavy leg work or while the legs are still sore (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: As in vertical jumping, the countermovement uses the [[term:ssc|stretch-shortening cycle]] [@Nicol2006_SSC]; the forward take-off angle shifts more of the work to the hip extensors (background biomechanics).
drills.evidence: Plyometric training improved countermovement jump height by 8.7% [@Markovic2007_vertjump], and standing long jump improved markedly with combat-sport training in non-athlete students (ES 1.04) [@HernandezMartinez2025_combatsports], so it responds to training. Dose and progression here are practical convention.

drills.name: Lateral bound (skater jump)
equipment: 3-4 m of clear, non-slip floor
drills.summary: You jump sideways from one leg to the other, like a speed skater, and hold each landing for 1 s. It trains sideways power and single-leg braking, the basis of change of direction.
drills.dose: 2 x 5 per side in the athletic lower-day warm-up, holding each landing 1 s, about 60-90 s between sets. Bound to the left first so the left leg takes the first landing. Each landing counts as one contact.
setup: Stand on the right leg, left foot off the floor, knee slightly bent.
Check there are at least 2 m clear on each side and nobody walking past.
execution: Push off the right leg and bound sideways to the left.
Land on the left leg with the knee bent over the toes and hips back; hold 1 s.
Let the right foot hover or touch lightly behind the left ankle.
Push off the left leg and bound back to the right. Keep the bounds short until landings are still.
cues: Land like a skater: soft, low, still.

errors.error: Knee collapsing inwards on landing.
errors.fix: Shorten the bound and push the knee out over the toes.

errors.error: Trunk tipping over the landing leg.
errors.fix: Keep the chest up over the hip and reduce the distance.

errors.error: Bounding again before the landing is still.
errors.fix: Count 'one' after each landing before pushing off.

drills.progression: Longer bounds; then continuous bounding with a shorter hold once landings are consistently stable.
drills.regression: Lateral step-and-hold, or two-foot hops sideways over a line.

alternatives.why: Change-of-direction work with less single-leg landing load.
Single-leg control without impact.

drills.whyChosen: Lifting and running are mostly forward-backward, while change of direction, martial-arts footwork and dance need sideways power and landing control (practical convention). The single-leg landings give your weaker left leg direct practice. Change of direction behaves as a task-specific skill [@NygaardFalch2019_COD], so sideways movement is trained directly. See [[dec:D17]] and [[dec:D28]].
drills.safety: Stop with knee or ankle pain. Use trainers with lateral support on a dry, non-slip floor; dusty or polished floors are a slipping risk (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: Each landing makes the gluteus medius and ankle stabilisers stop sideways momentum on one leg, an [[term:eccentric|eccentric]] braking action, followed by a [[term:ssc|stretch-shortening]] push-off [@Nicol2006_SSC]. Plyometric training improves balance tests about as much as balance training [@Ramachandran2021_plyobalance], probably through better-timed muscle activation (inference).
drills.evidence: In athletes, plyometric, strength, sprint and specific change-of-direction training all improved change-of-direction performance, with no form clearly superior [@NygaardFalch2019_COD]. Plyometric training improved dynamic balance (ES 0.50) [@Ramachandran2021_plyobalance]. No data on novice adults were found for this drill; dose and progression are practical convention.

drills.name: Medicine-ball throws (chest pass and rotational)

primary: chest, front shoulders and triceps (chest pass)

equipment: medicine ball 3-5 kg that rebounds predictably (a wall ball or rubber ball)
solid wall
drills.summary: Explosive throws of a medicine ball into a wall: a two-hand chest pass and a side-on rotational throw. They train upper-body and trunk power, the qualities behind punches and strikes in martial arts, without heavy load and without a partner.
drills.dose: 3 x 5 rotational throws per side (left side to the wall first) and 3 x 5 chest passes, about 60 s between sets, every throw at full intent. It is not in a fixed warm-up block: use it on upper or athletic days as the plan directs.
setup: Chest pass: stand 1.5-2 m from a solid wall, feet hip-width, ball at the chest.
Rotational throw: stand side-on about 1 m from the wall, left side towards it first, ball at hip height on the far side.
execution: Chest pass: lean in slightly and push the ball explosively from the chest into the wall at chest height; catch the rebound with soft elbows and reset.
Rotational throw: turn away from the wall to load the hips, then drive off the back foot, turning hips before shoulders, and throw the ball into the wall at hip-to-chest height.
Catch the rebound, reset fully and repeat.
End the set if throw speed drops.

errors.error: Throwing with the arms only on the rotational throw.
errors.fix: Pivot the back foot and let the hips turn before the shoulders.

errors.error: A ball so heavy that throws are slow.
errors.fix: Use a lighter ball; speed is the stimulus.

errors.error: Rounding the lower back to rotate.
errors.fix: Stand tall, brace and rotate around a vertical axis.

drills.progression: Stand further from the wall, then add a step into the throw; use a heavier ball only if throw speed stays high.
drills.regression: A lighter ball (2-3 kg), or submaximal throws to learn the sequence.

alternatives.why: Anti-rotation trunk strength without impact.
The upper-body strength base; plyometric push-ups come much later.

drills.whyChosen: Martial arts need fast force from the hips through the trunk to the hands, and a ball and a wall let you train that alone (practical convention). The rotational throw also adds a twisting pattern that most lifting lacks. See [[dec:D17]].
drills.safety: Use a solid, clear wall and check that nobody is nearby, since rebounds can be unpredictable. Do not use a ball with a split cover. Stop with shoulder, elbow or lower-back pain.
drills.mechanism: The wind-up pre-stretches the trunk and shoulder muscles just before release, a [[term:ssc|stretch-shortening cycle]] (inference by analogy with jumping [@Nicol2006_SSC]). Sequencing hips, trunk and arms passes momentum along the body, as in a punch (background biomechanics).
drills.evidence: No study in these catalogues tests medicine-ball throws; the plyometric evidence concerns jumping [@Markovic2007_vertjump], so applying it to throws is inference. Dose and the martial-arts rationale are practical convention.

drills.name: Agility ladder drills
equipment: agility ladder, or tape lines or floor markings about 45 cm apart
drills.summary: Quick, light footwork patterns through the squares of a floor ladder: two-feet-in, lateral in-out and the icky shuffle. A playful coordination warm-up before athletic work; on its own it mainly improves ladder skill rather than general agility.
drills.dose: 2 patterns x 3 passes in the athletic lower-day warm-up (about 2-3 min), walking back as recovery. Choose from two-feet-in, lateral in-out and icky shuffle, and rotate them every few weeks.
setup: Lay the ladder flat on a non-slip floor away from walkways; if the gym has none, mark 8-10 squares with tape.
Trainers on; start at one end.
execution: Two-feet-in: move forward placing both feet in each square, left foot first, then the right.
Lateral in-out: side-on to the ladder, step in-in, out-out along it, leading with the left first, then the right.
Icky shuffle: step in with one foot, follow with the other, step out to the side with the first, and continue diagonally forward, alternating sides.
Go slowly until the pattern is automatic, then speed up, staying on the balls of the feet.
cues: Eyes up once you know the pattern.

errors.error: Going fast and hitting the rungs.
errors.fix: Slow down until the pattern is clean; speed comes second.

errors.error: Looking down throughout.
errors.fix: Look at the far end once the pattern is learned.

errors.error: Flat-footed, heavy steps.
errors.fix: Stay on the balls of the feet with soft knees.

drills.progression: New patterns every few weeks for variety, then finish each pass with a short sprint or shuffle out of the ladder.
drills.regression: Walk the pattern, then jog it.

alternatives.why: Rhythm drills for running if there is no ladder.
Change-of-direction practice closer to real sport.

drills.whyChosen: It adds variety and a playful start to athletic days, which matters because boredom is your most likely reason to stop (practical convention). No study supports ladder work as a route to general agility, so it is kept short; learning a dance style or martial art is the more plausible route to coordination (inference). See [[dec:D17]].
drills.safety: A sliding ladder is a trip hazard: tape it down or use tape lines, and keep it out of walkways in a busy gym.
drills.mechanism: Repeating a pattern produces motor learning specific to that pattern. Transfer to other tasks is expected to be small, by analogy with balance training, where untrained tasks did not improve (SMD -0.07 to 0.18) [@Kummel2016_specificity] (inference).
drills.evidence: No meta-analysis or trial of agility-ladder training in adults was found; its use here is practical convention. Change-of-direction ability behaves as a task-specific skill [@NygaardFalch2019_COD]. The ACSM position stand recommends neuromotor (balance, agility, coordination) exercise on 2-3 days a week [@Garber2011_ACSM_position_stand].

drills.name: Cone shuffle and 5-10-5 drill
equipment: 3 cones, plates or water bottles 5 yd (4.6 m) apart
about 10 m of clear, non-slip floor
drills.summary: The pro-agility (5-10-5) drill: from the middle marker, go 5 yd to one side and touch the line, 10 yd back the other way and touch, then 5 yd back through the middle. It trains sideways acceleration, braking and turning with a low centre of mass.
drills.dose: 4-6 reps with full recovery (about 60-90 s, walking back). It is not in a fixed warm-up block: use it in change-of-direction work after a full warm-up, as the plan directs. Go left first on the first rep, then alternate.
setup: Place three markers in a line 5 yd (4.6 m) apart.
Stand at the middle marker at right angles to the line of markers, feet wider than the shoulders, knees bent, hips low.
execution: Push off and move 5 yd to the left (shuffle, or turn and sprint); touch the line with the left hand.
Brake in a low, wide stance, push off and go 10 yd to the right; touch the line with the right hand.
Turn and go 5 yd back through the middle marker.
Walk back and rest fully before the next rep.
cues: Low hips, wide base at the turn.

errors.error: Standing up tall before the turn, so braking takes longer.
errors.fix: Lower the hips and shorten the steps 1-2 m before the line.

errors.error: Crossing the feet during the shuffle.
errors.fix: Keep the feet apart and push off the trailing leg.

errors.error: Knee collapsing inwards on the plant.
errors.fix: Slow down and plant with the knee over the toes.

drills.progression: Faster reps once braking is controlled; later, reactive starts on a random audio or visual cue from an app, since you train alone.
drills.regression: Shorter distances (3-6-3 m) at moderate speed; shuffle only, no sprint.

alternatives.why: Sideways power and single-leg landing practice.
A gentler footwork warm-up.

drills.whyChosen: Change of direction is a task-specific skill [@NygaardFalch2019_COD], so practising the shuffle, brake and turn of real sport and martial-arts footwork trains it more directly than generic drills (inference). The fixed layout lets you time reps on your phone to see progress, although no norms or measurement-error data for it are in this programme's sources.
drills.safety: Warm up fully first, including running drills. Use trainers with lateral support on a dry, non-slip floor. Stop with groin, knee or ankle pain.
drills.mechanism: Each turn requires rapid [[term:eccentric|eccentric]] braking followed by a push-off the other way, a [[term:ssc|stretch-shortening]] action [@Nicol2006_SSC]; a low centre of mass and wide base shorten the braking distance (background biomechanics).
drills.evidence: In athletes, plyometric, strength, sprint and specific change-of-direction training all improved change-of-direction performance, with effects from about zero to large and no form clearly superior [@NygaardFalch2019_COD]. No evidence was found for untrained adults; dose and progression are practical convention.

drills.name: Resting heart rate (manual)
equipment: Phone stopwatch
Bed or chair
drills.summary: A 60-second pulse count on waking, taken on three mornings and averaged. It is a slow-moving marker of aerobic fitness and recovery, not a daily readiness score.
drills.dose: Three consecutive mornings in the week of each test session ([[phase:p0]] baseline and each reassessment); optionally one count a week in between for the [[plan:monitoring]] trend.
setup: Phone timer within reach, so you need not get up.
Pick one position and keep it: lying on your back before getting up, or seated after 5 min of quiet rest.
Before caffeine, food and screens.
execution: Place two fingertips (not the thumb) on the thumb side of the inner wrist, just below the base of the thumb.
Start the timer and count beats for a full 60 s.
Write the number down at once; repeat on the next two mornings and average the three.
cues: Light pressure: pressing hard can hide the pulse.

errors.error: Counting after walking about or after a coffee.
errors.fix: Count before moving, or after 5 min seated, before caffeine.

errors.error: Trusting one reading.
errors.fix: Use the 3-day mean; single readings are noisy.

errors.error: Counting for 15 s and multiplying by 4.
errors.fix: At rest use the full 60 s: each miscounted beat in a 15-s count is a 4-bpm error.

drills.progression: If you buy a wearable ([[dec:D25]]), its resting value can replace the manual count, provided you keep comparing the same device and the same metric.
drills.regression: If the wrist pulse is hard to find, use the neck (carotid) pulse with light pressure on one side only.

alternatives.why: Measures aerobic capacity through performance; resting heart rate is only a marker.

drills.whyChosen: It takes a minute, needs no equipment and gives context to the walking and running tests. You wake at about 12:00, so 'morning' here means on waking, about an hour before you train.
drills.safety: A resting value persistently above 100 bpm, an irregular rhythm, or palpitations with faintness or chest discomfort need a doctor's review (clinical convention; see [[plan:safety]]).
drills.mechanism: Resting cardiac output changes little with training, so a larger [[term:stroke-volume|stroke volume]] lets the heart deliver it at a lower rate; greater resting vagal tone contributes (mechanistic reasoning). Interval training raised stroke volume by about 10% in one trial in moderately trained men [@Helgerud2007_4x4RCT].
drills.evidence: Across prospective cohorts, each 10 bpm higher resting heart rate was associated with 17% higher all-cause mortality (RR 1.17, [[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 1.14-1.19) and 15% higher cardiovascular risk, with high heterogeneity; it is an observational marker, not a proven lever [@Aune2017_RHRmeta]. It is one of the four strongest predictors in a non-exercise [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] model [@Nes2011_nonexerciseVO2], and wrist optical sensors are reasonably accurate at rest [@Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy]. The counting protocol itself is practical convention.
protocol: Same position and the same point after waking every time, before caffeine and food.
Count for 60 s on three consecutive mornings; log each value and the mean.
Note poor sleep, alcohol, illness or a hot room on the previous night.
drills.scoring:
Score = mean of three 60-s counts (bpm).

Caffeine, short sleep, heat, illness, dehydration and alcohol all raise it acutely, so read only the 3-day mean and its trend across test sessions. With regular aerobic training a gradual fall over months is the expected direction (inference). A mean clearly above your usual, together with fatigue or a sore throat, points to illness or poor sleep rather than lost fitness ([[rule:illness]]). The sources reviewed give no minimal detectable change for a self-counted resting heart rate.

drills.name: Rockport 1-mile (1.6 km) walk test

secondary: Heart-rate response to a fixed task

equipment: Treadmill at 1% incline, or a flat measured 1.6 km route
Phone stopwatch
Chest strap, if you have one
drills.summary: Walk 1.6 km as fast as you can, then take your pulse at once. Time, heart rate, age, sex and body weight go into a published equation that estimates [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]], your maximal rate of oxygen use. The test is submaximal and low-risk, so it suits you before you run.
drills.dose: One attempt in the [[phase:p0]] baseline and [[phase:p1]] reassessment sessions; rest 10-15 min before the next test.
setup: Use the gym treadmill at 1% incline (practical convention); indoors avoids the 13:00 heat and is easier to repeat (inference).
Find the emergency stop and clip the safety key to your clothing.
Same shoes, and similar meal and caffeine timing, every time.
execution: After 5 min of easy walking, start the timer and walk 1.6 km as fast as you can: always one foot on the belt, no jogging, hands off the rails.
Raise the speed in steps over the first 400 m to the fastest pace you can hold, then hold it.
At 1.6 km stop the belt, find your pulse within 5 s, count for 15 s and multiply by 4 (or read the chest strap).
cues: Short, quick steps; drive the arms.

errors.error: Holding the handrails.
errors.fix: Let the arms swing; holding on reduces the work and invalidates the equation.

errors.error: A slow pulse count after stopping.
errors.fix: Heart rate falls quickly in recovery; have the timer ready and start within 5 s.

errors.error: Breaking into a jog.
errors.fix: Drop the speed slightly; the equation assumes walking.

drills.progression: Once you can run 20 min continuously, the 2.4 km run ([[ex:test-run-2400]]) replaces it from [[phase:p2]].
drills.regression: If brisk walking is uncomfortable, walk at your best steady pace and note it; the estimate is then a lower bound.

alternatives.why: More valid once you run, but maximal and dependent on pacing.
An input to non-exercise fitness estimates: no effort, but it tracks training change poorly.

drills.whyChosen: It estimates aerobic capacity without running or maximal effort, it was derived in adults aged 30-69 (you are 31), and you can do it alone on a treadmill [@Kline1987_Rockport]. It is the aerobic baseline behind [[dec:D11]].
drills.safety: Stop for chest pain or pressure, faintness, unusual breathlessness or palpitations ([[plan:safety]]).
drills.mechanism: Oxygen uptake equals cardiac output times the arteriovenous oxygen difference (the [[term:fick-principle|Fick principle]]). At a given walking speed a fitter person works at a smaller fraction of capacity, so heart rate is lower; a faster time at a lower heart rate implies a higher ceiling. That is the logic of the equation (mechanistic reasoning).
drills.evidence: In the derivation study, where subjects walked the mile as fast as possible at least twice, r = 0.93 with a standard error of estimate (SEE) of 0.325 L/min; on cross-validation r = 0.92, SEE 0.355 L/min (n = 169) [@Kline1987_Rockport]. No source reviewed reports within-person test-retest reliability. Each 1 [[term:met|MET]] of higher fitness was associated with 13% lower all-cause mortality (RR 0.87, [[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 0.84-0.90) [@Kodama2009_CRFmortalityMA]. A chest strap agreed almost perfectly with ECG (Lin rc 0.996) [@Gillinov2017_HRmonitors].
protocol: Same time after waking (about 13:00), same treadmill and incline, similar room temperature.
Five minutes of easy walking first; no lifting beforehand.
Record time to the second, heart rate, that morning's body weight and any deviation.
Log it in Hevy as distance and time, with heart rate in the notes ([[plan:logging]]).
drills.scoring:
Kline equation: VO₂max (L/min) = 6.9652 + 0.0091 × weight (lb) - 0.0257 × age (y) + 0.5955 × sex (1 = male) - 0.2240 × time (min) - 0.0115 × HR (bpm) [@Kline1987_Rockport]. Weight in lb = kg × 2.2046; time in decimal minutes (14:30 = 14.5); divide L/min by body mass in kg and multiply by 1000 for mL/kg/min.

At 77 kg, each minute faster adds about 2.9 mL/kg/min and each 10 bpm lower about 1.5. The SEE is about 4.6 mL/kg/min at your weight, so a single estimate is good to roughly ±9 (inference: 2 × SEE). Read the direction: a faster time at the same or lower heart rate, in the same conditions, is real improvement. The equation came from track walking, so a treadmill value may sit a little higher or lower; keep the set-up fixed (inference).

drills.name: 2.4 km (1.5-mile) run test

secondary: Running speed over a fixed distance

equipment: Treadmill at 1% incline (or a flat measured route or 400 m track)
Phone stopwatch
Chest strap, if you have one
drills.summary: Cover 2.4 km as fast as you can at an even pace and record the time. Among distance-based field tests it gives the most valid estimate of [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]], but it is a maximal, pacing-dependent effort, so it replaces the walking test only once you run comfortably.
drills.dose: One attempt in the [[phase:p2]] and [[phase:p3]] test sessions, once you can run 20 min continuously; rest 10-15 min before the next test. Until then, repeat the 1.6 km walk ([[ex:test-rockport]]).
setup: Use the same treadmill at 1% incline every time (practical convention); at 13:00, indoors is cooler and more repeatable than an outdoor route (inference).
Clip the safety key to your clothing and locate the stop button.
Same shoes, and a similar pre-session meal and caffeine timing as last time; no lifting before the test.
Warm up with 5-8 min of easy jogging and 2-3 short pick-ups ([[ex:wu-pickups]]).
execution: Set the belt to the fastest pace you believe you can hold for the whole distance and start the timer.
Change speed only in small steps (0.2-0.5 km/h), and not before 800 m; aim for even splits.
If you still have something left at 2.0 km, raise the speed for the last 400 m.
Stop the timer at 2.40 km, note your heart rate if you wear a strap, then walk easily for 5 min ([[ex:cd-easy]]).
cues: Even effort: the first kilometre should feel controlled.

errors.error: Starting too fast and fading.
errors.fix: Hold back for the first 800 m; aim for a second half no slower than the first.

errors.error: Holding the handrails.
errors.fix: Let the arms swing; holding on unloads you and flatters the time.

errors.error: Changing the course, incline or time after waking between tests.
errors.fix: Keep them fixed and write any deviation in the notes.

drills.progression: Training moves the result, not repeated testing: the 4 × 4 intervals ([[ex:cardio-int-4x4]]) and steady sessions ([[ex:cardio-steady]]) are the levers, progressed by [[rule:cardio-progression]].
drills.regression: If you cannot run the full distance, or a shin, calf or knee complaint is present, do the 1.6 km walk ([[ex:test-rockport]]) instead and follow [[rule:running]].

alternatives.why: Submaximal and walking only: the right test before you can run 20 min, or when running is off the table.
An effortless trend marker; it does not measure capacity.

drills.whyChosen: It had the highest validity of the distance-based walk/run tests [@MayorgaVega2016_walkrunMA], needs only a treadmill and a stopwatch, and you can do it alone. It waits for [[phase:p2]] because it is maximal and needs running fitness: novice runners are injured roughly twice as often per hour of running as established recreational runners (17.8 vs 7.7 injuries per 1000 h) [@Videbaek2015_runningInjuryIncidence]; see [[dec:D14]].
drills.safety: A maximal effort in a warm climate: drink normally beforehand, test indoors, and stop for chest pain or pressure, faintness, palpitations or unusual breathlessness ([[plan:safety]]). Do not test through a running niggle ([[rule:pain]]).
drills.mechanism: Over 2.4 km almost all the energy comes from aerobic metabolism, so your speed depends on [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]], the fraction of it you can sustain, and your running economy (mechanistic reasoning). The time therefore mixes capacity with pacing skill and economy, which is why the estimate is imperfect and why practice alone can take seconds off it (inference).
drills.evidence: In a meta-analysis of walk/run field tests, the 1.5-mile run correlated with measured VO₂max at rp 0.79 ([[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 0.73-0.85), similar to the 12-min run (0.78); sex, age and fitness level did not modify validity [@MayorgaVega2016_walkrunMA]. No source reviewed reports its within-person test-retest reliability. In one small trial in untrained men, 12 weeks of moderate continuous running (3 × 60 min a week) raised relative VO₂max by 21.5%, partly through about 6 kg of weight loss [@Milanovic2015_untrainedMenRunningRCT], so changes over months should be clearly visible (inference).
protocol: Same treadmill, 1% incline, similar room temperature, about 1 h after waking (13:00).
Standard warm-up: 5-8 min easy jogging plus 2-3 pick-ups; no lifting beforehand.
Run 2.4 km at the fastest even pace you can hold; record total time to the second, the 1.2 km split, and end heart rate if available.
Log it in Hevy as distance and time, with splits, heart rate and conditions in the notes ([[plan:logging]]).
drills.scoring:
Primary score: time (min:s); lower is better.

A commonly used conversion is VO₂max (mL/kg/min) ≈ 3.5 + 483 ÷ time (min) (practical convention: the equation is not among the sources reviewed and its error is unknown here). For example, 13:00 gives about 40.7 and 12:00 about 43.8, so near these times each minute faster is worth about 3 mL/kg/min.

With no published measurement error, treat a change smaller than about 2-3% of your time (roughly 15-25 s near 13 min) as possibly due to pacing, heat or sleep, and trust changes that repeat across tests (inference). Do not compare this estimate directly with your Rockport estimate: the equations differ, so switching tests can shift the number without any change in fitness (inference).

drills.name: Push-up test (max reps)

secondary: Trunk stiffness in the plank position

equipment: A fist-height marker (about 10 cm): a foam or yoga block, or a firmly rolled towel
Phone for side-on video
Exercise mat or rubber floor
drills.summary: One set of as many strict push-ups as you can do, each with the chest touching a fist-height marker and the arms locking out, stopping at the first rep that breaks the standard. It tracks upper-body pushing endurance; your baseline is 5.
drills.dose: One maximal set in each test session ([[phase:p0]] baseline, then [[phase:p1]], [[phase:p2]] and [[phase:p3]]), after the general warm-up; rest 3 min before the pull-up test.
setup: Hands just wider than the shoulders, fingers forward, feet together; note a floor reference (a tile edge or a strip of tape) so the hand position repeats.
Place the marker under your breastbone.
Prop the phone on the floor side-on to film; with no partner, the video is your judge (practical convention).
execution: Start at the top: arms straight, body in one line from head to heels, glutes and abdomen tight ([[term:bracing|bracing]]).
Lower under control until the chest touches the marker, elbows angled roughly 45° from the body (practical convention).
Press back to straight arms: one rep. Keep a steady rhythm without resting at the top or bottom.
Stop at the first rep that misses the marker or the lockout, lets the hips sag or pike, or follows a pause of more than about 2 s; that rep does not count.

errors.error: Hips sagging as fatigue builds.
errors.fix: Brace and squeeze the glutes; the first clear sag ends the test.

errors.error: Shallow reps near the end.
errors.fix: Only reps that touch the marker and lock out count; check the video.

errors.error: Hands wider or further forward than last time.
errors.fix: Use your floor reference so the hand position repeats.

drills.progression: Training happens in [[ex:push-up]] sets with [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]]; this test is your only planned push-up set to [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]].
drills.regression: If a wrist hurts on the floor, use push-up handles or hexagonal dumbbells as handles with the same marker standard; note it, and use the same set-up at every later test.

alternatives.why: The training exercise, with incline and loaded progressions; submaximal, not a test.
Optional trunk-endurance test in a similar body position.

drills.whyChosen: It needs no equipment, takes a minute and reflects the pushing work in your programme. It is also a crude health marker: in male firefighters, more than 40 push-ups versus fewer than 10 was associated with far fewer cardiovascular events over 10 years (incidence rate ratio 0.04, [[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 0.01-0.36) [@Yang2019_pushups]. Part of the baseline battery ([[dec:D03]]).
drills.safety: Stop for sharp wrist, elbow or shoulder pain ([[rule:pain]]). Breathe out on the way up rather than holding your breath through the set (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: A reps-to-failure test at a fixed submaximal load ends when fatigue (metabolite accumulation and falling force per contraction) leaves you unable to produce the force a rep needs (mechanistic reasoning). Early gains come mostly from [[term:neural-adaptation|neural adaptation]], better recruitment and coordination of [[term:motor-unit|motor units]], before muscle growth contributes much (mechanistic reasoning). Losing fat also makes each rep lighter (inference).
drills.evidence: A 15-s timed push-up test had very high reliability (intraclass correlation, ICC, 0.989) and a minimal detectable change of 2 reps [@Negrete2010_UEtestsMDC]; no source reviewed gives equivalent data for a maximal set, so this is the nearest guide. The firefighter association was adjusted for age and BMI but not for aerobic fitness and rested on few events, so it is a prognostic marker, not a target; your 5 reps sit in that cohort's lowest group [@Yang2019_pushups].
protocol: Same place in the session: after the general warm-up, before the pull-up test, with no pushing work beforehand.
Two easy reps as a primer, then 1-2 min rest (practical convention).
One maximal set to the standard above, filmed side-on; count only valid reps.
Log in Hevy as one bodyweight set at [[term:rpe|RPE]] 10 with 'test' in the notes ([[plan:logging]]).
drills.scoring:
Score = number of valid reps.

Taking the timed-test minimal detectable change of 2 reps as a guide [@Negrete2010_UEtestsMDC], a gain of 3 or more reps under the same standard is likely real (inference). Expect a quick rise from 5 in the first months: much of it is skill and neural adaptation rather than new muscle (inference). No norms in the sources reviewed match this protocol, so your own trend is the reference.

drills.name: Pull-up test (max reps)
equipment: Fixed pull-up bar (or the pull-up handles on a cable tower or assisted-dip machine)
Bench or box to reach the bar
Phone for side-on video
Chalk, if your gym allows it
drills.summary: One set of as many strict pull-ups as you can do, from a dead hang to chin over the bar, without swinging. Your baseline is 3. It measures pulling strength relative to body weight, which shapes the back and arms you are training for.
drills.dose: One maximal set in each test session, 3 min after the push-up test ([[phase:p0]] baseline, then [[phase:p1]], [[phase:p2]] and [[phase:p3]]).
setup: Overhand grip just outside shoulder width, thumbs wrapped around the bar; note the grip width (against the knurling or a mark) and repeat it every time.
Use the same bar each time.
Prop the phone side-on so the video shows your chin at the top and straight arms at the bottom.
execution: Step off the bench into a dead hang: arms fully straight, feet off the floor, legs still.
Pull until your chin is clearly above the bar, head level.
Lower under control to straight arms: one rep. Continue without kipping (no hip or leg drive) and without resting more than about 2 s at the bottom.
Stop at the first rep that fails to clear the bar, and step down onto the bench rather than dropping.
cues: Shoulders down from the ears, then elbows to the ribs.

errors.error: Bent arms at the bottom.
errors.fix: Straighten the elbows fully before each rep; the video settles disputes.

errors.error: Kicking or kipping for the last rep.
errors.fix: That rep does not count; the test ends there.

errors.error: Craning the neck to get the chin over.
errors.fix: Keep the head level; the chin must clear the bar without tilting.

drills.progression: Training uses [[ex:pull-up]] progressions (assisted and lowering-only, [[term:eccentric|eccentric]], reps) and [[ex:lat-pulldown]]; this test is the only planned maximal pull-up set.
drills.regression: On a day you cannot complete one rep (for example after illness), record 0 plus the seconds you take to lower slowly from the top, and note the reason (practical convention).

alternatives.why: A palms-facing grip lets the biceps help more; the scores are not interchangeable, so do not switch grips between tests.
The same movement pattern with adjustable load, for training; a pulldown set is not comparable with a pull-up test.

drills.whyChosen: It needs only a bar and directly measures pulling strength relative to body weight. Maximum-rep pull-ups were reliable from day to day within a test battery in conditioned soldiers [@Lester2014_pullupReliability]. Part of the baseline battery ([[dec:D03]]).
drills.safety: Step down rather than drop from the bar, and stop for sharp elbow or shoulder pain ([[rule:pain]]). Wrap the thumbs: a slipping grip is the usual cause of falls (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: At 3-5 reps this is closer to a strength test than an endurance test: each rep needs a large share of your maximal pulling force, and your body mass is the load (mechanistic reasoning). Early gains come mostly from [[term:neural-adaptation|neural adaptation]]; later gains from muscle growth and a lower fat mass (mechanistic reasoning; inference).
drills.evidence: In conditioned soldiers, a battery including maximum-rep pull-ups had between-day intraclass correlations (ICC) of 0.87-0.98, and averaging three trials raised it to 0.93-0.95 [@Lester2014_pullupReliability]. A modified pull-up test had a minimal detectable change of 2 reps [@Negrete2010_UEtestsMDC]. No civilian adult norms were found in the sources reviewed.
protocol: 3 min after the push-up test; same bar and grip width every time.
Dead-hang start, chin over the bar, straight arms between reps, no kipping.
Stop at the first failed rep or a rest of more than about 2 s; count valid reps from the video.
Log in Hevy as one bodyweight set at [[term:rpe|RPE]] 10, with grip width, that morning's body weight and 'test' in the notes ([[plan:logging]]).
drills.scoring:
Score = number of valid reps.

Using the 2-rep minimal detectable change of a related test as a guide [@Negrete2010_UEtestsMDC], a change of 1-2 reps may be noise, while 3 or more is likely real (inference). Body weight changes the load: 3 kg of fat lost makes every rep about 4% lighter at 77 kg, so read the score beside your weight (inference). No norms in the sources reviewed apply, so your own trend is the reference.

drills.name: Plank hold test (optional)
equipment: Exercise mat
Phone filming side-on (stopwatch in view, or use the video timer)
drills.summary: Hold a forearm plank in a straight line for as long as good form lasts. Your baseline is 60 s. The test is optional: beyond about a minute the score reflects tolerance of discomfort more than anything your programme targets (inference).
drills.dose: Optional and not part of the planned test sessions. If you do it, once per test session and last in the battery, so it cannot tire the trunk before other tests (practical convention).
setup: Forearms on the mat, elbows under the shoulders, forearms parallel.
Feet hip-width apart, on the toes.
Phone on the floor side-on, filming, so you can judge your line and read the time afterwards.
execution: Lift the hips until the body forms a straight line from head to heels, then start timing.
Breathe steadily and hold the line.
Stop when the hips sag or pike visibly, a knee touches down, or you can no longer hold the line; record the time.
cues: Ribs down, slight tuck of the pelvis.
Push the floor away with the forearms.

errors.error: Hips sagging into the lower back.
errors.fix: Tuck the pelvis slightly and squeeze the glutes; the first clear sag ends the test.

errors.error: Hips rising into a pike.
errors.fix: Check the video; the standard is a straight line.

errors.error: Holding the breath.
errors.fix: Breathe steadily; breath-holding makes the hold harder and ends it early (inference).

drills.progression: For training, harder variations beat longer holds: the long-lever progressions in [[ex:plank]], plus [[ex:side-plank]] (practical convention).
drills.regression: If your lower back aches during the hold, stop, note the time and train trunk control with [[ex:dead-bug]] instead; see [[rule:pain]].

alternatives.why: The training exercise, progressed by lever length rather than hold time.
Trains the lateral trunk, which a front plank barely tests.
Trunk control with movement and little load on the back.

drills.whyChosen: You already have a 60-s baseline and the test costs a minute, so it is available if you want a simple trunk-endurance marker. It stays optional because none of your goals depends on holding a plank for longer (inference).
drills.safety: Breathe throughout rather than straining against a held breath (the [[term:valsalva|Valsalva manoeuvre]]) during a long hold, and stop for back pain ([[rule:pain]]).
drills.mechanism: A plank is an [[term:isometric|isometric]] contraction: the trunk muscles stop gravity from extending your spine without the joints moving. In a sustained contraction the muscle's own pressure limits its blood flow, metabolites accumulate and force capacity declines until form fails (mechanistic reasoning). Where the hold ends also depends on the shoulders, the hip flexors and how much discomfort you accept, so the score is only a loose marker of trunk strength (inference).
drills.evidence: The sources reviewed contain no validity, reliability or normative data for the plank hold, so this test rests on practical convention; that is why it is optional.
protocol: If done, last in the test session; same mat, elbow and foot positions.
Film side-on; start timing once the line is set.
Stop at the first clear loss of the straight line and record the seconds.
Log in Hevy as a timed set with 'test' in the notes ([[plan:logging]]).
drills.scoring:
Score = seconds held with a straight line.

The sources reviewed give no minimal detectable change, and the end point depends on judgement and motivation, so only a large change that repeats across tests means much (inference). Better trunk control shows more clearly as harder plank variations in training than as a longer hold.

drills.name: Standing broad jump test
equipment: Tape measure (3 m or longer)
Masking tape for a take-off line
A clear, non-slip strip about 4 m long (turf or rubber flooring)
Phone for side-on video
drills.summary: From a standing start, jump forward as far as you can off both feet, land without falling back, and measure from the take-off line to the back of the nearer heel. Best of 3 counts. It is the power test in your battery; strength training and [[term:plyometrics|plyometrics]] should raise it.
drills.dose: Three attempts, best counts, in each test session ([[phase:p0]] to [[phase:p3]]), 60-90 s apart (practical convention). If you can, practise 3-5 jumps at the end of the warm-up on two training days before the baseline.
setup: Stick a strip of masking tape on the floor as the take-off line and fix the tape measure alongside it, zero at the line's front edge.
Same floor and shoes each time; in a busy gym, use the turf or functional area at a quiet moment.
Prop the phone side-on at the landing zone so you can read the heel position against the tape.
execution: Toes just behind the line, feet about hip-width apart.
Swing the arms back as you dip into a quick partial squat, then swing them forward hard and jump forward and up, extending hips, knees and ankles together.
Land on both feet with the knees bending to absorb, and hold the landing for 2 s; if you fall back or touch down with a hand, repeat the attempt.
Measure from the take-off line to the back of the heel nearer the line, to the nearest centimetre; check the video if unsure.
cues: Arms back, then drive them forward.
Stick the landing: soft knees, chest up.

errors.error: Falling backwards on landing, which shortens the mark.
errors.fix: Land with the hips back and the arms forward; repeat any attempt you cannot hold for 2 s.

errors.error: Shuffling or stepping before take-off.
errors.fix: Both feet stay planted until take-off; a step voids the attempt.

errors.error: Knees caving inward on landing.
errors.fix: Land with the knees over the middle of the feet, and jump a little shorter until landing control improves.

drills.progression: Power is trained with [[ex:plyo-broad-jump]] and [[ex:plyo-box-jump]] (low volume, full recovery) alongside strength work; three test jumps are not a training stimulus.
drills.regression: If a knee, ankle or back complaint makes landing uncomfortable, skip the test and note why ([[rule:pain]]); do not substitute a vertical jump, which is not comparable.

alternatives.why: The training drill: submaximal sets with full recovery, not a scored test.
Trains vertical power with a smaller landing load, since you step down.

drills.whyChosen: It is the only power test in your battery, it needs only a tape, and in 410 adults it reflected laboratory horizontal power and force together with body composition [@MarinJimenez2024_SLJ]. It tracks the athletic qualities in [[dec:D17]].
drills.safety: Jump only after the general warm-up and a few progressive practice jumps, on a dry non-slip surface, never on loose mats. Stop for knee, ankle or Achilles pain ([[rule:pain]]).
drills.mechanism: The quick dip before take-off uses the [[term:ssc|stretch-shortening cycle]]: stretching the active hip, knee and ankle extensors just before they shorten adds stored elastic energy and stronger activation to the push (mechanistic reasoning). Distance depends on take-off velocity, which depends on the force you produce in a fraction of a second relative to your body mass, so strength, practice and a lower fat mass all help (mechanistic reasoning).
drills.evidence: In the Adult-Fit study, jump distance was explained by laboratory maximal horizontal power, sex, body-fat percentage, maximal horizontal force and lean mass (R = 0.78). On first exposure the retest was on average 12.1 cm longer (intraclass correlation, ICC, 0.94; coefficient of variation 7.1%; minimal detectable change 29 cm); after a learning period the retest difference was 0.45 cm (ICC 1.00; CV 0.5%; MDC 1 cm) [@MarinJimenez2024_SLJ].
protocol: Same floor, shoes and line set-up, after the general warm-up and 2-3 progressive practice jumps.
Three counted attempts, 60-90 s apart; feet planted until take-off; hold each landing for 2 s.
Measure from the line to the back of the nearer heel; repeat any attempt with a fall-back or a hand touch.
Log all three and the best in Hevy notes ([[plan:logging]]).
drills.scoring:
Score = best of 3, in cm.

Newcomers gain about 12 cm on the first retest from learning alone, and until the jump is familiar the minimal detectable change is about 29 cm; after familiarisation it falls to about 1 cm [@MarinJimenez2024_SLJ]. Read the [[phase:p0]]-to-[[phase:p1]] change as mostly learning unless you practised beforehand. After that, changes of more than a few centimetres are probably real (inference: reading your own mark from video adds error that trained testers avoid). Fat loss alone can lengthen the jump, since body-fat percentage was one of the predictors (inference).

drills.name: Single-leg stance test

primary: Static single-leg balance, eyes open and eyes closed

equipment: Firm, flat floor (not a mat); barefoot
A wall or rack within reach
Phone for video timing
drills.summary: Stand on one leg with your hands on your hips, first with eyes open and then with eyes closed, for up to 45 s; best of 3 for each leg and condition. It measures the left-side deficit in your baseline (right 30 s eyes open and 15 s eyes closed; left 20 s and 10 s) that [[dec:D28]] targets.
drills.dose: Each leg, eyes open and eyes closed, best of 3 with a 45-s cap, in each test session ([[phase:p0]] baseline, then [[phase:p1]], [[phase:p2]] and [[phase:p3]]). Left leg first in each condition.
setup: Barefoot on the same firm floor, near a wall or rack you could touch if you lost balance, but not touching it.
Pick a fixed point on a wall at eye level, about 2 m away, for the eyes-open trials.
Film every trial and read the time afterwards: with your hands on your hips you cannot work a stopwatch.
execution: Hands on hips. Stand on the left leg and lift the right foot so it is near, but not touching, the left ankle; timing starts when the foot leaves the floor.
Hold for up to 45 s. The trial ends when the standing foot shifts or pivots, the raised foot touches down or touches the standing leg, a hand leaves the hip, or (eyes closed) you open your eyes.
Alternate legs (left, then right) for 3 trials each with eyes open, then repeat with eyes closed, closing your eyes only once you are steady.
cues: Spread the toes and feel the whole foot.
Quiet upper body; let the ankle make the small corrections.

errors.error: Resting the raised foot on the standing leg.
