errors.fix: Keep it near the ankle without contact; contact ends the trial.

errors.error: Peeking during eyes-closed trials.
errors.fix: Close the eyes once steady and keep them closed; opening them ends the trial.

errors.error: Testing in shoes or on a mat.
errors.fix: Barefoot on the same firm floor every time; the surface changes the score (inference).

drills.progression: Improve the score through [[ex:bal-sls]] and [[ex:bal-sl-reach]] practice and unilateral strength work such as [[ex:split-squat]] and [[ex:sl-rdl]], left side first.
drills.regression: If eyes-closed trials make you stumble, do them standing in a corner so the walls can catch you, with the same rules.

alternatives.why: The training version of the same task, with harder variations.
Dynamic single-leg control; trained, but not scored in the battery.

drills.whyChosen: It needs no equipment, the best-of-3 score is highly reliable, and there are published values for your age group [@Springer2007_unipedalstance]. It turns your left-right gap into a number you can track.
drills.safety: Low risk: stand within reach of support and clear of equipment.
drills.mechanism: Upright balance integrates vision, the vestibular system and [[term:proprioception|proprioception]] from muscle spindles and joint receptors, mostly around the ankle. Closing the eyes removes vision, so eyes-closed scores lean on proprioceptive and vestibular input (mechanistic reasoning). Practice refines the small ankle and hip corrections, often within weeks (inference).
drills.evidence: In men aged 18-39 tested barefoot with arms crossed on the chest (45 s maximum, 3 trials), eyes-open best of 3 averaged 44.4 s (SD 4.1) and eyes-closed 16.9 s (SD 13.9); inter-rater reliability of the best-of-3 score was excellent (intraclass correlation 0.994-0.998) [@Springer2007_unipedalstance]. Your baseline eyes-open values, though not taken with this exact protocol, sit well below that mean, whereas your eyes-closed values lie within the wide normal spread. Balance (proprioception) training reduced sports injuries in a meta-analysis of trials (risk ratio 0.55, [[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 0.35-0.87) [@Lauersen2014_injury_prevention].
protocol: After the general warm-up; barefoot; same floor and wall target.
Order: eyes open left, right, left, right, left, right; then eyes closed in the same order.
Film each trial and read the time from the video; stop at 45 s.
Log the best of 3 for each leg and condition in Hevy notes ([[plan:logging]]).
drills.scoring:
Score = best of 3 (s) in four cells: left and right, eyes open and closed. Also compute the asymmetry, left ÷ right × 100 (baseline 67% in both conditions).

The norms used arms crossed on the chest; hands on hips is similar, but compare with them only loosely (inference). The sources reviewed give no minimal detectable change, and eyes-closed scores vary widely between people (SD 13.9 s), so treat changes of a few seconds as noise and look for a trend over two tests (inference). Reaching 45 s eyes open on both legs is the realistic first target; after that, the eyes-closed scores and the asymmetry are the numbers that matter (inference).

drills.name: Fingertip-to-floor (toe-touch) test

primary: Combined hamstring, hip and lower-back forward-bending range

equipment: Tape measure fixed vertically to the front of a box or bench end (zero at the floor)
A sturdy step or low plyo box, once your fingertips pass the floor
Phone for side-on video
drills.summary: Stand with your knees straight, bend forward slowly as far as you can, and measure the distance from your middle fingertip to the floor: positive above the floor, negative below it. It is a simple, highly reliable measure of whole-chain forward bending, and the number behind your toe-touch goal ([[dec:D27]]).
drills.dose: Two attempts, record the better, in each test session ([[phase:p0]] baseline, then [[phase:p1]], [[phase:p2]] and [[phase:p3]]).
setup: Test about 1 h after waking (13:00), after the same general warm-up and before any stretching: warm-up and time of day alone shift flexibility by 2-3 cm [@Edwards2026_diurnal_flexibility].
Barefoot, feet together, toes against the box or bench end carrying the vertical tape, so you can read your fingertips against it.
Once you pass the floor, stand on a step with the tape fixed to its front face, zero at the standing surface, reading downwards.
execution: Knees straight but not forced back, arms hanging, middle fingers together.
Breathe out and roll forward slowly, reaching straight down; no bouncing.
Hold the lowest point for 2 s and read (or film) the distance from the middle fingertips to the floor or step surface.
Stand up, wait 15-20 s, repeat once and record the better value.
cues: Let the head and neck hang.
Knees straight, weight over the middle of the feet.

errors.error: Bending the knees at the bottom.
errors.fix: Film side-on; a bent knee voids the attempt.

errors.error: Bouncing for extra range.
errors.fix: Move slowly and hold 2 s; a bounced reach is not comparable.

errors.error: Testing cold, after stretching, or at a different time after waking.
errors.fix: Same warm-up, before stretching, about 1 h after waking.

drills.progression: The hamstring stretches ([[ex:st-ham-supine]], [[ex:st-ham-bench]]) and full-range hinges such as [[ex:db-rdl]] drive the change: in a meta-analysis, resistance training improved range of motion about as much as stretching [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM].
drills.regression: If bending forward hurts your back, skip the test and note it; the supine strap position ([[ex:st-ham-supine]]) lets you follow hamstring range with the back supported ([[rule:pain]]).

alternatives.why: A straight-leg raise in this position is more hamstring-specific and reliable (minimal detectable difference 6-7°) [@Neto2015_AKE_SLR_reliability], but measuring the angle alone needs a phone-inclinometer set-up.

drills.whyChosen: It needs only a tape, it measures exactly the limitation you described, and it has excellent reliability and responsiveness [@Perret2001_fingertip_floor_test]. The sit-and-reach was not chosen because its validity for hamstring extensibility is only moderate [@Mayorga2014_sit_and_reach_validity].
drills.safety: Stop if bending forward causes back pain, or pain or tingling down a leg: that points to nerve or spinal irritation rather than tight muscle and needs review ([[plan:safety]]; clinical convention).
drills.mechanism: The test measures the whole forward-bending chain: hip flexion (limited mainly by the hamstrings), lumbar flexion and the mobility of the sciatic nerve, not hamstring length alone (mechanistic reasoning). Over weeks of stretching, most of the gain comes from greater [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]]: you accept more tension before stopping, while muscle stiffness and architecture change little [@Magnusson1996_stretch_tolerance; @Freitas2018_chronic_stretch_mechanics].
drills.evidence: In patients with chronic low-back pain, fingertip-to-floor distance correlated with radiographic trunk flexion at r = -0.96, intra- and inter-observer reliability were excellent (intraclass correlation 0.99) and responsiveness was high (standardised response mean 0.97) [@Perret2001_fingertip_floor_test]; no source reviewed gives its error in healthy adults. Whole-body flexibility varied by 3.0 cm between 08:00 and 20:00, peaking around 16:00, and a 30-min warm-up added about 2.4 cm over a 5-min one [@Edwards2026_diurnal_flexibility].
protocol: About 1 h after waking, after the standard general warm-up, before any stretching.
Barefoot, feet together, toes against the tape box (or on the step once you pass the floor).
Two slow reaches 15-20 s apart, each held 2 s; film side-on to check the knees.
Record the better value in cm (positive above the floor, negative below) in Hevy notes ([[plan:logging]]).
drills.scoring:
Score = better of 2 attempts, in cm from middle fingertip to floor; lower is better, and negative means past the floor.

With no minimal detectable change for healthy adults in the sources reviewed, and warm-up and time of day alone shifting flexibility by 2-3 cm [@Edwards2026_diurnal_flexibility], treat changes under about 3 cm as possible noise (inference). Testing an hour after waking probably catches you near your least flexible point, so never compare with an evening attempt (inference). Fingertips level with the tips of your toes corresponds to a score of a few centimetres, and 0 cm means touching the floor (inference). Gains in the first weeks mostly reflect stretch tolerance, which is still usable range (inference).

drills.name: Knee-to-wall ankle test

secondary: Calf (soleus and gastrocnemius) and Achilles extensibility

equipment: A clear wall
Tape measure
Masking tape
Phone for video
drills.summary: Facing a wall in a lunge, find the furthest your foot can be from the wall while the knee still touches it and the heel stays down; that toe-to-wall distance is the score. It is a reliable measure of the ankle range that governs squat depth and how far the knee can travel forward.
drills.dose: Each side, best of 3, in each test session ([[phase:p0]] baseline, then [[phase:p1]], [[phase:p2]] and [[phase:p3]]); left side first.
setup: Stick a strip of masking tape on the floor at right angles to the wall and fix the tape measure along it, zero at the wall.
Barefoot, same wall and floor each time, after the general warm-up and before any calf stretching.
Prop the phone side-on and low, so the video shows your heel and the knee touching the wall.
execution: Left foot on the tape line, big toe and heel on the line so the foot points straight at the wall; right foot behind for balance, hands on the wall.
Drive the knee forward over the second toe to touch the wall without lifting the heel.

If the knee touches easily, slide the foot back about 1 cm and retry; if the heel lifts or the knee misses, move it forward. The trial score is the greatest big-toe-to-wall distance at which the knee touches with the heel down.
Three trials per side, alternating left and right.

errors.error: Heel lifting at the end.
errors.fix: Check the video; a lifted heel voids the trial.

errors.error: Knee falling inward to reach the wall.
errors.fix: Keep the knee tracking over the second toe; collapsing inward borrows range from the foot (mechanistic reasoning).

errors.error: Foot turned out.
errors.fix: Keep the big toe and heel on the line.

drills.progression: Improve it with [[ex:st-calf-wall]] (straight and bent knee) and [[ex:wu-ankle-rock]], and use the new range in deep squats such as [[ex:goblet-squat]].
drills.regression: If the front of the ankle pinches before the calf feels stretched, stop at the pinch, record that distance and note it; recurring pinching is a pain question, not a stretching target ([[rule:pain]]).

alternatives.why: The warm-up drill in the same position: practice, not a measurement.

drills.whyChosen: Ankle dorsiflexion limits how far the knee can travel forward in squats, split squats and landings, and you can measure it alone in two minutes. The weight-bearing lunge test has good reliability and a known minimal detectable change [@Powden2015_WBLT_reliability].
drills.safety: Low risk. Keep a hand on the wall, and stop for Achilles or ankle pain ([[rule:pain]]).
drills.mechanism: With the heel down, the knee can move forward only as far as the shin can rotate over the ankle (talus). That is limited mainly by the extensibility of the calf and Achilles tendon, and sometimes by bony contact at the front of the joint (mechanistic reasoning). Because the knee is bent, the two-joint gastrocnemius is slackened, so the test mostly reflects the soleus and the joint itself (mechanistic reasoning).
drills.evidence: A systematic review found good inter-clinician (intraclass correlation 0.80-0.99) and intra-clinician (0.65-0.99) reliability, with a minimal detectable change of about 1.6 cm between testers and 1.9 cm for the same tester [@Powden2015_WBLT_reliability]. Calf stretching does change dorsiflexion: muscle-directed stretching added 7.3° ([[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] 4.1-10.5) [@Andrade2020_muscle_nerve_stretching], and 4 weeks of high-intensity calf stretching raised range by 40%, versus 15% with low intensity [@Nakamura2021_HI_vs_LI_SS].
protocol: After the general warm-up and before calf stretching; barefoot; same wall.
Left side first; three trials per side, alternating.
Each trial: the greatest toe-to-wall distance with the knee touching and the heel down, checked on video.
Log the best for each side, to the nearest 0.5 cm, in Hevy notes ([[plan:logging]]).
drills.scoring:
Score = best of 3 per side, in cm.

Because you test yourself, use the same-tester minimal detectable change of about 2 cm [@Powden2015_WBLT_reliability]: a change of more than 2 cm on a side, or a left-right difference of more than 2 cm, is probably real (inference from that figure). The sources reviewed give no norms, so compare yourself with yourself and read the two sides together, alongside how deep and upright your squats feel.

drills.name: Tape measurements and progress photos

secondary: Chest, arm, thigh, hip and neck girths

equipment: Non-stretch tape measure (a fibreglass tailor's 'inch tape' is fine)
Mirror
Phone on a shelf or small tripod, with self-timer
The same room and lighting each time
drills.summary: Waist at two sites every week, a full set of girths monthly, and monthly photos under fixed conditions. With body weight, these are your most practical way to see whether you are losing fat and gaining muscle; the scale alone cannot separate the two ([[dec:D23]]).
drills.dose: Waist (navel and narrowest point): weekly. Full set and photos: monthly. Always on waking (about 12:00), after using the toilet, before food, drink and training.
setup: Underwear only, standing relaxed in front of a mirror, feet together, weight even.
Tape horizontal all the way round (check in the mirror), snug on the skin without denting it.
Take waist readings at the end of a normal breath out; do not pull the belly in.
execution: Every week: waist at the navel (the site the [[term:navy-method|US Navy method]] uses) and at the narrowest point between ribs and hips.

Monthly, in this order: neck (just below the Adam's apple), chest (nipple line), both waist sites, hips (widest point of the buttocks), shoulders (around the widest point of the deltoids, arms relaxed at the sides), upper arm (largest point, relaxed and then flexed) and thigh (15 cm above the top of the kneecap), left side first (sites by practical convention).
Take each site twice; if the readings differ by more than 1 cm, take a third and use the middle value (practical convention). Record to 0.5 cm.
Photos: phone at chest height, 2-3 m away, on the same spot, with the self-timer; front, side and back, relaxed, in the same underwear and light.

errors.error: Mixing the two waist sites.
errors.fix: Your navel and narrowest readings differ by about 5 cm (86 vs 81 cm), so label each and never compare across sites.

errors.error: Measuring after a meal or a workout.
errors.fix: Measure on waking, before eating or training; food, fluid and the post-training pump all enlarge girths for hours (inference).

errors.error: Pulling the tape tighter for a better number.
errors.fix: Same snug tension every time; check in the mirror.

drills.progression: Once a month, enter waist, neck, height and weight into [[tool:bodycomp]], which turns them into body-fat ranges (US Navy method and [[term:rfm|relative fat mass]]).
drills.regression: If the full set becomes a chore, keep the two waist sites, body weight and photos; they carry most of the information (inference).
drills.whyChosen: Waist tracks the fat you want to lose, and arm, chest and thigh girths track the muscle you want to gain; together they separate the two in a way body weight cannot (inference). [[term:whtr|Waist-to-height ratio (WHtR)]] discriminated cardiometabolic risk better than BMI or waist alone [@Ashwell2012_WHtR], and Asian Indian men carry risk at smaller waists than Western cut-offs assume [@Misra2006_IndianWaist].
drills.safety: No physical risk. Keep the photos private, and if measuring starts to feed anxiety about your body, measure less often (inference; see [[sci:sci-behaviour]]).
drills.mechanism: Waist circumference rises and falls mainly with abdominal (subcutaneous and visceral) fat, so it is the most direct tape marker of fat change; limb girths mix muscle and fat, so a rising arm or thigh girth with a steady or falling waist suggests muscle gain (mechanistic reasoning; inference).
drills.evidence: Studies measure waist at the minimal waist, the midpoint between lowest rib and iliac crest, or the navel; risk associations were similar across sites [@Ross2008_waistprotocol], but absolute values differ, so one site must be used consistently. WHtR improved discrimination of hypertension, diabetes and cardiovascular disease by about 4-5% (area under the curve) over BMI [@Ashwell2012_WHtR]. In Asian Indian men a waist of 78 cm identified at least one cardiovascular risk factor (sensitivity 74.3%, specificity 68.0%) [@Misra2006_IndianWaist]. Recent food and fluid shift anthropometric estimates, and unstandardised conditions distort measured change [@Kerr2017_foodfluid; @Tinsley2021_trackingchange]. No study reviewed validates progress photos judged by eye; the nearest evidence is an industry-linked algorithm that estimated body fat from standardised smartphone photos (men: concordance with [[term:dxa|DXA]] scans, CCC 0.90) [@Nana2022_footBIAvsDXA].
protocol: On waking (about 12:00), after the toilet, before food, drink and training; underwear only; same room and mirror.
Weekly: both waist sites, 2 readings each. Monthly: the full set, left side first.
Monthly photos with a fixed spot, distance, phone height, light and poses.
Log girths in Hevy's body measurements (or notes), with anything unusual such as a late salty meal, illness or festival food ([[plan:logging]]; [[plan:monitoring]]).
drills.scoring:
Record each site in cm (to 0.5 cm). Waist-to-height ratio = navel waist ÷ height; yours is about 86 ÷ 181 = 0.475.

| Marker | Reference |
|---|---|
| WHtR | 0.4-0.49 healthy; 0.5-0.59 increased; 0.6 or more high [@NICE2025_NG246] |
| Waist, Asian Indian men | action level 1 at 78 cm, level 2 at 90 cm [@Misra2006_IndianWaist] |

At 86 cm you sit between the two Indian action levels, while your WHtR is below 0.5. No source reviewed quantifies the error of self-measured waist, so read trends, not single readings: a change of about 1 cm or less between two measurements is within ordinary technique and gut-content variation (inference). While gaining muscle, a sustained rise in navel waist across several readings is the earliest sign that fat gain is outpacing muscle gain; while losing fat, a falling waist with steady or rising arm and thigh girths is the pattern you want (inference). Photos are a qualitative record and are never turned into numbers.

drills.name: Easy cardio warm-up without equipment

secondary: calves and ankles (jogging on the spot, skipping)

equipment: none: about 2 × 2 m of floor, or a staircase
optional: a skipping rope (from Phase 2)
drills.summary: Continuous easy-to-moderate movement that opens every [[phase:pa|Away-mode]] session in place of the gym's bike or rower: marching on the spot, walking up and down stairs, or, from [[phase:p2]], jogging on the spot or easy skipping. Its job is the same as [[ex:wu-cardio-easy]]: raise muscle temperature, heart rate and breathing before anything else, which matters for you because you train about an hour after waking.
drills.dose: Strength sessions: 4 min, starting easy ([[term:rpe|RPE]] 2–3) and finishing moderate (RPE 4–5). Steady session: 5 min of walking that builds to brisk. Interval session: 8 min (4 min easy, then 4 min moderate at RPE 5). Take 1–2 min longer on cold days or when you feel stiff. Logging it in Hevy is optional; if you do, use a cardio entry with the minutes.
setup: Clear about 2 × 2 m of floor, or use a lit staircase with a handrail where you will not block anyone.
Wear shoes on a hard or slippery floor; socks slip on tiles (practical convention).
A phone timer or the app's timer is enough; no heart-rate monitor needed.
execution: First half easy (RPE 2–3): march on the spot with a relaxed arm swing, or walk up and down one or two flights at an easy pace, holding the rail on the way down.

Second half: lift the knees higher and quicken the rhythm, or climb a little faster, until breathing is clearly faster but full sentences are still possible (RPE 4–5). From Phase 2, easy jogging on the spot or skipping can replace the marching.
Go straight on to the mobility drills without sitting down.

errors.error: Turning it into a workout, such as racing up the stairs (RPE 7 or more).
errors.fix: Cap it at RPE 5; the job is temperature, not fitness.

errors.error: Jumping or jogging on the spot in Phase 1 because it warms you faster.
errors.fix: March or walk stairs instead; the programme adds impact gradually from Phase 2 (practical convention).

errors.error: Skipping it because the room is hot.
errors.fix: A warm room is not working muscle: passive heating was largely ineffective as an upper-body warm-up [@McCrary2015_upperbody_warmup].

drills.progression: No load progression. As fitness improves, the same RPE needs a quicker rhythm, higher knees or faster stairs; follow RPE, not the clock.
drills.regression: Stay at RPE 2–4 throughout, marching slowly, if 4 min leaves you breathless.

alternatives.why: The machine version: use it whenever a bike, rower, cross-trainer or treadmill is available (a hotel gym counts).
From [[phase:p2]], if you packed a rope, easy skipping can be the second half.

drills.whyChosen: It does the job of the gym's machine warm-up with nothing but floor or stairs. In one study of 56 adults, performance (grip strength was the only physical test) followed biological time and habitual sleep timing rather than clock time [@FacerChilds2018_chronotype], so a session an hour after waking probably behaves like an early-morning one (applying this to you is inference), and warm-ups reduced such time-of-day differences across studies [@Kusumoto2021_diurnal_variation]. Marching and stair walking come first because they add little impact (practical convention). See [[dec:D30]].
drills.safety: Hold the rail on stairs and keep the descent slow (practical convention). For chest pain, dizziness, palpitations or unusual breathlessness, stop and follow [[plan:safety]]. In hot weather stay at RPE 4–5 and drink water (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: As with the gym version, warmer muscle speeds cross-bridge cycling and nerve conduction and resists lengthening less (background physiology, not measured in the cited trials). Temperature is only part of it: in a small study, an extended morning warm-up that raised rectal temperature to evening levels did not restore evening lifting performance [@Pullinger2019_morning_warmup_lifts], so rehearsal and neural activation probably matter too (inference).
drills.evidence: Warm-ups improved performance in 79% of outcomes across 32 studies, with little sign of harm [@Fradkin2010_warmup_performance]; adding 20 min of easy cycling to a specific warm-up raised leg-press [[term:1rm|1RM]] by 8.4% in 13 trained people [@Abad2011_general_specific_warmup]. Warm-ups reduced time-of-day performance differences, an extended morning warm-up most [@Kusumoto2021_diurnal_variation]. No study in these sources compares marching or stair walking with machine cardio as a warm-up; treating them as equivalent at the same RPE is inference.

drills.name: No-equipment intervals (stairs, hill or bodyweight circuit)
drills.system: Aerobic: high-intensity intervals without a machine
equipment: a stairwell of several floors (default), a hill, or a safe running route
or about 2 × 2 m of non-slip floor and a sturdy step for the circuit
interval timer (the app's)
drills.summary: Your Away-mode interval session: 2-min hard efforts with 2 min easy between, done by climbing stairs, walking uphill (or running, if your phase already includes it) or, in a room with neither, a low-impact bodyweight circuit. Hard means [[term:rpe|RPE]] 8–9, only a few words possible by the end of each effort, not all-out. It keeps the job of your gym intervals ([[ex:cardio-int-4x4]]) while you are away.
drills.dose: [[phase:pa]] week 1: 4 × 2:00 hard (RPE 8–9) / 2:00 easy; weeks 2–3: 6 × 2:00 hard / 2:00 easy. Warm up with [[ex:wu-cardio-noeq]] (8 min) and two pick-ups, and finish with [[ex:cd-easy]]; about 40 min in all. If your gym phase has no intervals yet (Phase 0, or Phase 1 before week 7), do a steady session instead; in the rest of Phase 1, keep the hard efforts at RPE 7–8, as in your gym intervals (practical convention).
setup: Choose the mode in this order: stairs, a hill, running (only if your phase already includes running, see [[rule:running]]), then the circuit.
Stairs: a quiet, lit stairwell with a handrail. A building of about 10 storeys suits a 2-min climb at a hard pace (practical convention). Check that the stairwell doors will let you back in.
Circuit: clear about 2 × 2 m of non-slip floor and find a bottom stair or a sturdy step about 15–20 cm high.
Set the app's interval timer to 2:00 hard / 2:00 easy for the week's number of efforts.
execution: Each hard effort: settle into a pace you expect to hold for 2 min; by the end you should be at RPE 8–9, able to say only a few words.

Stairs: climb steadily, one step at a time, using the rail lightly for balance. Recover by walking down easily, holding the rail. With only a few floors, climb and turn back down continuously and push only on the way up.
Hill: walk briskly, or run if running is part of your phase, uphill for 2 min; walk back down for the recovery.

Circuit: each 2-min effort is 30 s each of high knees (fast marching with high knees in Phase 1), mountain climbers, fast step-ups (alternate the leading leg) and squat to calf raise, moving straight from one to the next; then 2 min of easy marching. From [[phase:p2]], and only if your knees and calves tolerate them, jumping jacks, squat jumps or burpees can replace one or two moves.
Pace evenly so the last effort matches the first (floors climbed or reps done); log the mode, efforts completed and session RPE.

errors.error: Sprinting the first flights and crawling the last.
errors.fix: Start each effort slightly below target; the effort climbs on its own as the 2 min pass.

errors.error: Hurrying down the stairs to save time.
errors.fix: The walk down is the recovery: descend slowly, holding the rail.

errors.error: A circuit that never gets past RPE 6–7.
errors.fix: Move faster and through a fuller range, use a higher step, or find stairs. Only one of the pooled trials of bodyweight circuits recorded intensity, and low intensity may be one reason they improved cardiorespiratory fitness less than running or cycling training [@Scoubeau2022_wholeBodyHIITmeta] (inference).

drills.progression: Four efforts in week 1 of each trip and six in weeks 2–3; then hold six while output rises: more floors per effort, a steeper hill or a faster pace. For the circuit, move faster or, from Phase 2, swap in jumping moves.
drills.regression: Fewer efforts (3–4) or RPE 7–8 if you finish wrecked, sleep poorly or your next strength session suffers. After illness, follow [[rule:illness]] before any hard efforts.

alternatives.why: The machine version: use it whenever a bike, rower or treadmill is available (a hotel gym counts).
A brisk walk or hike instead when you are under-recovered or have no safe place for hard efforts. If you are ill, [[rule:illness]] decides whether you train at all.

drills.whyChosen: Stairs and hills come first because climbing reaches a high intensity at walking speed (biomechanical reasoning), and stair climbing, unlike hill walking, has been tested directly. Bodyweight-only [[term:hiit|HIIT]] improved cardiorespiratory fitness less than running or cycling training (intervals or continuous) in pooled trials [@Scoubeau2022_wholeBodyHIITmeta], whereas in one small trial in 15 sedentary young women (8 climbers, 7 controls) a programme of ~2-min ascents of a 199-step staircase at 90 steps a minute, building to 5 a day on 5 days a week over 8 weeks, raised [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] by 17.1% relative to controls [@Boreham2005_stairClimbing]. Two-minute efforts fit an ordinary stairwell or hill and fall within the longer-interval (≥2 min) format linked to larger VO₂max gains [@Wen2019_HIITprotocolsMA]; 4-min climbs would need a very tall building (practical convention). The circuit uses low-impact moves until Phase 2 because the programme adds impact gradually (practical convention). See [[dec:D30]].
drills.safety: The hardest session you do alone away from home: keep your phone with you, tell someone where you are, and stop for chest pain, faintness, palpitations or unusual breathlessness ([[plan:safety]]). Never run down stairs. Walking down is eccentric work for the thighs, so expect some thigh soreness after the first stair session (muscle physiology); week 1's four efforts allow for that. In Indian midday heat, use an indoor stairwell or shade and carry water (practical convention).
drills.mechanism: As with [[ex:cardio-int-4x4]], minutes near maximal heart rate load the heart's pumping capacity (standard physiology). Climbing lifts your whole body mass with every step, so stairs reach a high intensity at walking speed (biomechanical reasoning). A bodyweight circuit spreads the work over more, smaller muscle groups; that may be why it improved musculoskeletal fitness more, and cardiorespiratory fitness less, than running or cycling training in pooled trials [@Scoubeau2022_wholeBodyHIITmeta] (the explanation is inference).
drills.evidence: Across 19 trials (657 mostly healthy adults), bodyweight-only HIIT versus no exercise improved cardiorespiratory fitness ([[term:smd|SMD]] 0.75, 95% CI 0.28–1.23), fat-free mass (0.38) and musculoskeletal fitness (0.84). Versus running or cycling HIIT or continuous training it improved cardiorespiratory fitness less (−0.40, −0.70 to −0.11) but musculoskeletal fitness more (0.42); effects grew with total training time, and very short (4–7 min) protocols often failed to raise VO₂max [@Scoubeau2022_wholeBodyHIITmeta]. In a tiny trial (about 7 recreationally active young women per group), 4-min all-out bodyweight sessions 4 times a week raised VO₂peak about 8% in 4 weeks [@McRae2012_wholeBodyTabata], but in a larger trial of 68 young adults (mostly women) the same format improved time to fatigue and 5-km time at first yet kept no benefit at a 2-month follow-up, unlike about 30 min of vigorous running [@Islam2019_TabataVsVICT]. Stair protocols raised VO₂peak by 12% (3 × 20-s all-out climbs) and 7% (3 × 60 s up and down one flight) over 6 weeks in small uncontrolled trials in sedentary young women [@Allison2017_stairSprintSIT]. In trials of healthy adults and patients, home-based HIIT raised VO₂peak by 1.75 mL/kg/min versus no exercise but about 1.46 mL/kg/min less than laboratory HIIT [@Tsuji2023_homeHIITmeta]. See [[sci:sci-noequip]].
